1.	Where is Canada's collection, of war paintings stored and are they safely housed as regards possible damage from dampness or discoloration?
2.	Are they now so stored or placed that they can be seen by visitors to or residents of Ottawa ?

3.	What steps are now being taken or in contemplation by the government to provide for the permanent housing and proper display of such Canadian war paintings?

1.	The Canadian war memorials, except those pictures now hanging on the walls of the Senate chamber, are stored in a fire proof storage room, specially prepared under the supervision of the national gallery officials, in the Auditorium building. The pictures arc completely protected from any damage due to dampness or any other unfavourable atmospheric condition.
2.	The pictures, except as noted above, are not on exhibition at present, but they can be examined by special arrangement.
3.	When construction of a new national gallery building is undertaken provision will be made for the proper housing and display of the Canadian war memorials.

Summary of Customs Regulations respecting Export Entries of goods required to be observed by Shippers and Railway Carriers in Canada, when goods are laden at inland railway stations and sidings and consigned for exportation from Canada.

2.	The Export Entry may be signed by the shipper or his agent (who may also be the railway agent) in the presence of a witness, and is not required to be attested to.
3.	Goods for exportation are classed in the Export Entry Form as "Domestic Articles" or "Foreign Articles," Goods exported from a Customs Bonded Warehouse are to be reported on the same form (B. 13) but under the heading "Foreign Articles".

4.	Export Entries are required for coin or bullion exported, as in the case of other exports.

Remember that the Export Entries in duplicate for statistical purposes as above stated and as ordered by the Governor in .Council are to be delivered by the carrier of the goods to the Collector of National Revenue at the port of exit from Canada (being the last port in Canada through which the goods for exportation pass outwards for places beyond the limits of Canada when exported by land); and that it is most important to have the Export Entries furnished and firmly attached to the way-bill from inland places in order to avoid the necessity for detention and side-tracking of the goods at the frontier until Export Entries therefore are obtained and delivered to the Canadian Customs-Excise Officer.

PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN Am OF CONSTRUCTION

Mr. Speaker, the resolution now before the house is practically the same as that introduced by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner)

National Highways-Mr. Simpson
last session. At that time considerable discussion took place and many arguments were presented favouring the adoption of the resolution, at least in its amended form, but apparently we were not able to convince the government of the advisability of taking the desired action. In the interim the government may have had an opportunity of further considering the arguments that were then advanced, and the representations which, I believe, have been made (by the Canadian Motor League and other public bodies asking for federal assistance to highways. May we hope that as a result of this further consideration the government may be in a more receptive mood this session than they were when the resolution was first introduced, for I can assure them that the question of improved highways and improved roads connecting rural sections with those highways is one of supreme importance to the people of this country to-day.	'
The automobile to-day cannot be considered a luxury, it is a necessity. The professional man, the merchant, the contractor, the agriculturist, all make use of the automobile. If you visit the farmers' market on market day in any of our towns or cities and see the number of automobiles and motor trucks assembled there, you will be convinced of the necessity of the automobile to the agriculturist and the market gardener. Many of these producers have to travel miles to meet the consumers and dispose of their produce to the best advantage, for cash, a privilege which they did not enjoy before the advent of the motor and the improvement of the highways.
The government stated last year-I do not know whether they are of the same opinion this session or not-that this was a provincial matter, and that it was not a good principle for one government to collect taxes and another government to spend them, in fact, it was put in stronger language than that. It was said that it was a vicious principle. But I contend that the question of interprovincial highways, or a trans-Canada or national highway, is one that should be considered and that the project should be assisted by the federal government of this country. If the federal government relieves the provincial legislatures of the expenditures in that connection they will then be enabled more promptly to take care of the roads in the rural sections, and put them in such a condition that the agriculturists will be able to get their produce to the market. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that one of the most important things the government of this country can undertake to-day is

the completion of the trans-Canada highway. This government receives millions of dollars each year in customs duties, and in excise or luxury taxes on automobiles. Why should it not spend some of that money in the improving of the highways that are used by those automobiles? The tourist trade is surely one of national importance, and it has been increasing rapidly in recent years, at the same time becoming a very important source of revenue for the Dominion government. I cannot do better than quote from the annual address of Mr. Neill, the vice-president and managing director of the Royal Bank of Canada to the shareholders of that bank:
There is a tendency for the industries of a new country to rest upon the direct exploita-tion_ of natural resources. It is obvious that mining depletes mineral resources. To a somewhat lesser degree the same is true concerning our present methods of forestry which permit fire and cutting to destroy more than the year's normal growth, and a like statement may be made regarding the type of farming which takes away essential elements from the soil without effort at adequate replacement. It may be considered as evidence ef relative economic maturity that the individual Canadian industry which had the greatest growth in revenue between 1922 and 1929 was not dependent upon the destruction of our natural resources.
During this period, the value of the Canar dian tourist trade has grown at a more rapid rate than the income of any other individual industry in the country. According to the following table, published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the revenue from this source increased from ninety million dollars in 1922 to two hundred and fifty million dollars in 1928. Three hundred million dollars constitutes a conservative estimate of the total for 1929. On this basis there has been an increase of 233 per cent in this revenue since
He states further:
There is a greater annual migration across the border between Canada and the United States than across any other international boundary. During 1920 there were more than fifteen million people who visited Canada. The number of visitors in the course of the year is 50 per cent in excess of our total population.
We can only hope to increase this trade by improving our national highways, and by making accessible the beauty spots of this country, and I contend, Mr. Speaker, that in no way can that be more readily done than by completing the trans-Canada highway. We have, it is true, many beauty spots from one end of this country to the other, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia, but the portion of the trans-Canada highway that is not yet completed lies largely in northern Ontario, and I venture to say that there is no part of Canada that will be more attractive to the tourist than that undeveloped portion of northern Ontario through which that highway

National Highways-Mr. Carmichael
has not yet been completed. The tourists from the other side of the line who visit Canada naturally are anxious to get back into the primitive parts of the country, close to the natural beauty spots, and when they return home they not only return determined to come back but they tell their friends about it and in that way the tourist trade from the United States is increased year by year.
This portion of the trans-Canada highway is a fairly expensive portion to construct, but that is no reason why its completion should not be undertaken. As my hon. friend (Mr. Kellner) stated, years ago when the first railway was projected across Canada it was a tremendous undertaking, and some very stron-g criticism was offered at that time, but we all realize to-d'ay that had not that railway been constructed across Canada it is very doubtful if we would have a united Canada to-day. It has played a very important part in binding together the different parts of the Dominion. But to-day we are living not only in a railway age but in an age where more and more the people are travelling by automobile, and I think it is fair to assert that nothing to-day will do more to bind Canada together than the completion of the trans-Oanada highway, which would enable the people of the east to take their families in their motor cars and visit western Canada, and the people of the west to visit the east. In that way the people would become more and more familiar with their own country, and with conditions prevailing in different parts of the country. In that connection, Roger W. Babson, in speaking the other day with respect to the tourist business of the United States, had this to say:
An estimate of all expenditures in 1929 by tourists, vacationists, campers, etc., is about $4.000,009,000. Most of this money mas spent in the United States. Only 21 per cent of it, or $860,090,000, was spent in foreign countries. Hence the tourist trade is essentially a domestic industry, and one of great magnitude and importance. Its total value is about 41 per cent of our total national income. Its stimulating effects spread out over scores of other trades and industries. Retail business, gas and oil, sporting goods, wearing apparel, automobiles, garages, hotels, restaurants, amusement places, in fact, all business in the localities affected feel its beneficial influence.
As I stated before, many of our people in days gone by felt that they could not afford to take their families on long trips when the journey had to be made by railway, but today they have automobiles and are enabled to go on vacations of from ten days to two weeks. Where are they forced to go? In many cases, they are forced to cross the line, and they spend their money over there. If we had a trans-Canada highway, why would
not the same principle apply as that applied by Mr. Roger Babson to the United States? Instead of these people crossing the line and spending their money in the United States, they would travel to the west and leave their money in Canada.
I do not intend to argue this point at length. If the government will look upon this question in a reasonable way, if they sense at all public opinion on this matter they will give it more favorable consideration than was given last year. In my opinion, no other question involving the expenditure of a few millions of dollars would be more favourably received by the Canadian people than the expenditure necessary for the completion of the trans-Canada highway.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution now before the house is one of great importance. During the last session we had a lengthy discussion upon a similar resolution with an amendment, and while it was not carried by the house, it received a very substantial vote of this house. I do not think that vote was representative of the public opinion back of the resolution, but it was very substantial nevertheless.
In listening to the debate upon the resolution as proposed by the hon. member for Atha-baska (Mr. Kellner) I became convinced that he was asking more for a trans-Canada highway than for grants to aid provincial roads. In fact, after he had been speaking for a short time, I made a note, "some arguments for the trans-Canada highway" and later on I changed that to, "a good deal of argument for the trans-Canada highway." The last speaker (Mr. Simpson) has followed along the same line, putting forth the argument that we should have a trans-Canada highway. I, also, propose to take that line of argument, that Canada is in need of a transcontinental motor highway. The time is past due when steps should have been taken to build such a road.
We have in this country over one million motor cars, and during recent years our population has begun largely to move about by that method of transportation. As has been stated, a great many people desire to go from east to west and from west to east, but it is impossible to do so by motor car without the necessity of travelling through another country. That seems to me to be rather an uncalled for situation.
According to the annual report of the Royal Bank of Canada, approximately 15,000,000 visitors come to Canada annually and it is estimated that each visitor leaves about $1, or a total of $60,000,000. Along with the
430	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Carmichael
building of a trans-Canada highway we should advertise our country as a mecca for tourist traffic, and thus increase the sale of our Canadian goods.
It is figured that each visitor to France purchases about $750 worth of goods in that country, and the French government, appreciating that tourist trade and the revenue derived therefrom, have appropriated more than $1,* 000,000 for advertising purposes. Mr. Neill, who has been already quoted, stated at the Royal Bank annual meeting that if Canada sold only one-tenth of the amount of goods which France sells to each tourist, it would make a difference of over one billion dollars in our trade balance. I do not think we realize the tremendous possibilities there are in connection with the tourist trade, but the above figures will give some idea.
At the present time the provinces are putting forth considerable effort in the building of trans-provincial roads. It is possible to get across the entire province of British Columbia upon a good motor road, except for ferry transportation of a few miles across a small lake. I am informed that within a couple of years there will be another road across that province, which will be an allmotor highway. In the prairie provinces steps are being taken toward the rapid completion of provincial routes. In my own province of Saskatchewan the Minister of Highways has outlined a program which will bring about within the course of a few years the completion of three trans-provincial all-weather highways. I presume Manitoba is taking similar steps to build highways across that province, while the province of Quebec seems to be well advanced in that regard. I have the report for 1920 of the Department of Highways, in which the minister says:
The trans-Canada highway, whose completion is demanded with so much insistence by the western provinces, has been completed for several years as far as the province of Quebec is concerned.
The 1928 report of the Department of Highways for the province of Nova Scotia, while not dealing specifically with the trans-Canada highway, states:
The need for further federal aid for highways in this province is therefore imperative, and should be forthcoming to us in accordance with the spirit of the federal statute of 1919. and in view of the immense revenues collected by the Dominion government from Nova Scotia in federal taxes on the motor vehicle industry.
That quotation gives us some idea of how the different provinces view this project. It was stated last year and repeated this year in debate that there are approximately 600 miles necessary to complete a motor road

from coast to coast. It is possible that in time the individual provinces may have sufficient roadway completed to make a trans-Canada highway, but if left to the individual action of the various provinces it is hardly probable that we will have one continuous highway across Canada. For instance, in my own province we are to have three trans-provincial roads which may or may not connect with the Manitoba trans-provincial road and may or may not connect with the Alberta trans-provincial road. It is easy to see that when each province moves as an individual unit it is going to build a road that will suit its own convenience. It would seem almost imperative that there should be some unifying command that would coordinate the road building policy of the various provinces. Where should we look for that, other than to the federal parliament? There has been and still is a great deal of money spent in connection with roads. Up to the year 1928 we built 381,976 miles of highway in Canada; during the year 1928 there was spent on construction alone $38,912,000; and on maintenance of those highways in the same year the sum of $18,963,000 was spent, making a total of almost $58,000,000 for road construction and maintenance.
This money must be raised by direct or indirect taxation. The provinces have two ways of raising money that might be applied more particularly to road construction:	They collect from the registration of motor cars and from the sale of gasoline. In the year 1928 the sum of $191004,276 was collected by all the provinces for the registration of motor cars; in the same year $12,547,073 was collected for gasoline tax, making a total of $31,551,349.
I am giving these figures accurately because I wish to compare them with the figures that may be applicable to the federal government for expenditure on road improvement. This money a matter of $31,500,000, is collected provincially and as noted in previous figures almost $58,000,000 is spent on road improvement. Our Dominion government has a source of revenue from import duties on motor vehicles and parts, and during the year 1928 that government collected $24,961,099 from this source; in the same year it collected $2,977,375 through excise taxes on motor vehicles and parts, a total of $27,938,474.
Those are some figures which should appear to be rather convincing. Our nine provinces, combined, collected about $31,500,000 in revenue from the licences of motor cars and the tax on gasoline sales. Our Dominion government collects almost $28,000,000 from duties on motor vehicles and excise taxes on motor cars imported into Canada. Surely,

National Highways-Mr. Carmichael
Mr. Speaker, it is not unreasonable on the part of this House to ask that in view of the large revenue directly attributable to the motor car industry the Dominion government should not only give serious and favourable consideration to the resolution proposing aid to the various provinces, but should take action to see that there is a trans-Canada highway speedily completed across Canada.
I have here a resolution proposed by the Alberta Motor Association. I think it is representative of the majority of motorists in Canada, and represents the sentiment of the associations throughout the various provinces, if such associations exist. I would like to put this on record, as it has not been read into Hansard up to this stage. It reads as follows:
Whereas the members of the Alberta Motor Association believe that the association represents the opinion of the motorist in the province of Alberta;	_ _
And whereas increased facilities of transportation connecting all the provinces of Canada will tend to unify growth and bring about a better understanding between the parts thereof and induce a greater number of American tourists to visit Canada and thereby bring a great contribution of additional revenue to the public treasury, and will enable the Canadian motorist to obtain greater use of his investment in the automobile and will in many other ways contribute to the prosperity of Canada and the building of the nation;
And whereas in the opinion of this association a trans-Canada highway connecting all the provinces and extending from the Pacific to the Atlantic should be built at the expense of the Dominion government;
Therefore be it resolved that this association petition the government of Canada to commence as speedily as possible and carry to a rapid completion a trans-Canada highway.
In 1927 we had what was called a Dominion-provincial conference and I have here a precis of the discussions which took place at that time. I should like to place on record the opinions of the representatives gathered together at that conference. There were eighteen Dominion representatives, twenty-eight representatives from the nine provinces and nineteen other officials and advisers,, making a total gathering of sixty-five. Here is the statement of conclusions arrived at at that conference in regard to the subject of highway construction:
On the question of aid for highway construction practically aill the provinces, with the exception of Quebec, favoured (assistance from the federal treasury. It was pointed out that for some years such assistance had been given, but it had been discontinued. In the meantime with the increase in motor traffic the highway had become more and more a national undertaking, benefitting the Dominion as well as the provinces, and creating a new system of trade and commerce. The construction of these highways was a heavy burden upon some of the
provinces particularly, though the creation of those highways was saving much money to the treasury of the Dominion by reason of their taking the place of branch railway lines. It was estimated that $150,000,000 per year was being spent by tourists in Canada passing over the highways and that much of this money went into the federal treasury.
That represents the opinion expressed at the Dominion-provincial conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not all of it.

Not all of the
opinion? I note the province of Saskatchewan from which the Minister of Finance comes is represented in that expression of opinion; at least, so far as I have read, there is nothing to the countrary. It seems to me that federal action in this matter is long overdue. I thought, when I first came to Ottawa nearly nine years ago, we should be very careful of our expenditures, and I stilll think so. But I believe now perhaps I was over-careful when I see the money that can be found for less important expenditures than the one now before the house, and when I think of the large sums, the millions of dollars, that have been and are being spent on beautifying the capital city, without any hon. member raising objection to such expenditures. We have built a large hotel on a park and utilized the space there and we have torn down another large hotel to make a park where that hotel stood. We are building very fine roadways, magnificent bridges and improving the Rideau canal. We are doing pretty well for the city of Ottawa, but there are a number of taxpayers in the Dominion of Canada who would like to get some of the money that is being expended. Very few of the 10,000,000 people of this country will enjoy the benefits of the money we are expending in the capital city; but if we spent a portion of our money on a trans-Canada highway we would extend the privilege to many more citizens to enjoy such expenditures. If we have, as is stated, more than 1,000,000 motor -cars in Canada, that will represent perhaps one-half of our entire population. In other words, almost one-half of our population moves around in motor cars. If we had a trans-Canada highway, a large part of our population would be able to take advantage of it.
I would like to see some of this money running into several millions, I think, which is being expended in encouraging immigrants to come to Canada, spent on improving conditions and facilities in our own country. I believe the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) mentioned recently that there is to be no more assisted immigration into

National Highways-Mr. Carmichael
Canada. That was an encouraging statement. I hope the government is back of it That means there will be probably $3,000,000 that can be diverted from that expenditure to something more useful. What more useful expenditure could we engage in than that of building a trans-Canada highway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend sure of his figures?
I am not sure of what was spent last year, but a couple of years ago the total expenditure for immigration was $3,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend a minute ago said "assisted immigration". He said that we were going to drop $3,000,000 in connection with assisted immigration.
Three million dollars was spent in encouraging immigrants to come to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is very far wrong in that statement.

I am not speaking of assisted immigration from the British Isles; I am speaking of the total amount spent for immigration purposes which runs into around $3,000,000. Possibly it was more than that last year. An hon. member suggests that it is $3,500,000, so I am a little low instead of being a little too high. If we are to curtail our expenditures for immigration purposes, we might enlarge our expenditures for improving conditions at home. If we get our own people thoroughly satisfied and contented, and the conditions under which they labour congenial, we shall not have much trouble keeping them in Canada. I know from my district in recent years, many people have motored from Saskatchewan to Ontario. I am sure they would prefer motoring across Canada, but they were compelled to go through the United States.
I would like to commend the resolution to the serious consideration of the government.
I am not so much concerned about giving the donation to the provinces to spend haphazardly, but I would like to see a coordinating policy adopted by the Dominion government so that our transprovincial roads might be so dovetailed together and so continuous in construction that eventually we might have a trans-Canada highway from coast to coast.

Mr. Speaker, since this matter was before the house last year, there has been an almost universal expression of opinion from the

various parts of the Dominion in favour of building a highway from coast to coast and in support of the proposition that such a highway is a necessity. The Prime Minister last year, in answering the speakers in the debate along the same lines as the one now proceeding, said that he was opposed to the motion in that it brought forward an entirely vicious principle, that is, the principle of giving grants to the provinces outside of the subsidies to them. I might point out to the right hon. gentleman and to the house, that for many years or at least since the inception of the Dominion, federal grants have been made for railway purposes. The charters for those roads were granted by the Dominion government in each and every case where the railway crossed an intenprovincial boundary or an international boundary, and in many cases where they did not cross such 'boundary. Under conditions as they first existed, a grant generally of $6,400 per mile was made for such railways and no objection was taken. It was a continuous practice in Canada in those days for the development of the railways. To-day, in a great degree, our highways are taking the place of our railways. Our freights are being carried for short distances, and in some cases, for considerable distances, over provincial and other highways of the Dominion. In fact, even our railway companies-and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) will corroborate me in this-are to-day using provincial highways especially in the province of Ontario for the carrying of passengers and express for the benefit of the railways. I would also point out that the government has made at all times and does to-day make grants for interprovincial 'bridges, not for international bridges, but for bridges to connect highways between the various provinces.
The Dominion government is also making grants, and we shall vote them again this year as usual, for telegraph lines which are entirely within one province, in practically each case. I think there is in Canada only one interprovincial telegraph line maintained by the government, but in the great majority of cases the telegraph lines maintained and supported by the government for years past, have been and are entirely provincial in character.
The government is also supporting a system of dams along the streams for the benefit of the lumbering industry. They are entirely provincial, having absolutely no connection in any possible way with any other province or provinces. The government has also given assistance during the last year or two, to a

National Highways-Mr. Arthurs
provincial highway. This was after the amount granted in 1919 for highways had been expended. This was to assist the building of a highway in British Columbia. I am not saying the government is wrong, but I am pointing out to the minister that in each of these cases they have been doing exactly or approximately the act which would be committed if they gave assistance to the construction of a federal highway.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What particular highway is that?

A highway from Banff
to the coast. I do not remember the name of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We are
giving no grant to the provincial government there.

But the government is
building it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is going
through the park.

But the minister intends
to deal with it outside the park

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

That is exactly what I
am saying:	the government is building or
helping to build a road outside government land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: For the very good reason that we cannot go through the park, and we are willing to contribute our share.

The minister is probably
right. I am not saying that he is wrong in any one of these cases. I am not maintaining that the government is wrong in keeping up telegraph lines for the Yukon or elsewhere. I am simply pointing out what the minister has just admitted, that these grants are absolutely necessary, and I contend that a grant for a federal highway is equally necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We are
simply doing our share in our own territory.

Not through your own
territory.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I will deal
with that.

All right. A federal grant was made in the year 1919 for highways throughout the Dominion, and I would point out again this year, as I did last, that that grant was practically the first direct move towards good highways in the Dominion
of Canada; so much so, in fact, that in some cases the provinces were very unwilling to accept the grant even after it had been made. I can safely say that a couple of years elapsed before most of the provinces accepted that grant which had been voted by parliament, but to-day every one of the provinces, although slow to enter the scheme, sees the benefit of it and each and every one of the provinces is anxious that this government should continue the assistance which was then given.
One of the previous speakers has mentioned the amount of money that was spent on highways in 1928. I have in my room figures of the expenditure for 1929; I am sorry they are not here, but I would point out to the government that the expenditures by the provinces for this purpose have been very large and are increasing year by year, the lead being given by the province of Ontario, I will take the figure given for 1928 by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). He gave the figure as approximately $58,000,000. The revenue received by the provinces directly from the roads-I might point out that the revenue to the provinces is derived almost entirely from direct taxation for road purposes, such as the licensing of automobiles, and the gasoline tax-amounted to $31,000,000. In other words, the various provinces in Canada during that year, 1928, paid out $27,000,000 more than they received.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What proportion of that $58,000,000 was borrowed capital?

I am not talking about
that at all. It does not make any difference whether the provinces borrowed it or not; they have to pay it; it is no responsibility of this government at all. During the same period the revenue of this Dominion from the sales and luxury tax on automobiles was given by the hon. member for Kindersley as $28,000,000, with nothing spent on highways.
Let us take the example of the United States. That country is faced in many ways with the same difficulties that confront this Dominion. There are certain matters which are controlled entirely by the federal government of the United States, and certain others which are controlled entirely by the various states of the union, and certain other matters which are controlled in part federally, and in part by the state governments. The principle has been accepted in the United States that one of the matters over which there may be joint control and joint contributions is good roads. The United States a few years ago passed a vote of $75,000,000 a

National Highways-Mr. Arthurs
year for ten years for the establishment of highways in the United States; I am speaking of the federal government at Washington. This vote had nothing to do with the grants made by the various states. The Senate has passed an appropriation of $125,000,000 a year for three years, without regard to but in,elusive of the grants previously made. I think that appropriation has been voted by congress. In other words, the people of the United States are granting for road purposes federally, just as we are appealing to this government to grant federally, the sum of one dollar per head. If we take their population ait the very highest possible figure, 120,000,000, the United States are this year spending $125,000,000, or more than one dollar per head for assisting in the building of good roads in the United States. What is the present situation in the United States? To my knowledge, they have at least six highways stretching from ocean to ocean. They have over 200 highways, I think, but I will be conservative and say approximately 200 highways, of a national character outside of these six transcontinental highways. In Canada we have no such highway, and I contend that it is practically impossible for the various provinces of Canada, particularly the province of Ontario, which stretches such a tong distance from east to west, and a great deal of which comprises territory that is uninhabited and can only, foe used for mining and tourist purposes, to undertake a project of this kind, and federal assistance should be given in some way commensurate with the assistance given in the United States. If for instance the people of Canada should vote $9,000,000 a year for three years, we would not be spending one cent more than the people of the United States are spending federally per head for roads, and they already have 200 or more highways which are practically of the same character as our best Ontario provincial highways, and our Ontario highways are the standard in Canada. In addition, the United States have also six transcontinental highways, and I therefore think that we should be prepared to contribute as much per head as the people of the United States, and possibly twice as much if the necessity arises.
A good deal has been said here to-day regarding the benefits to be derived from such assistance for highways. I am pointing out that this assistance would benefit everybody. The first and probably one of the largest benefits would accrue to the federal government, because such a highway would bring into Canada a large number of tourists, and we would be able to exploit what is practically rMr. Arthurs.]
unknown territory so far as tourists are con-cemed. These tourists carry out of Canada a large quantity of goods manufactured in this country and we would benefit in that way. The provinces would also benefit. They would benefit by the tax upon gasoline and other taxes along that line; individuals would benefit, as pointed out by the member for West Algoma (Mr. Simpson). In short, everybody is concerned in this matter, and I think the government would be wise to accede to the request of ninety per cent of the people of Canada, and this year devote a substantial grant in assisting to establish a highway of this nature.
Hon, R. J. MANIO'N (Fort William): Mr. Speaker, for the last few minutes I have been hurriedly looking over the debate which took place last session on a similar resolution moved by the same hon. member from Athabaska (Mr. Kellner); and by the way, I think he deserves our applause for bringing this subject once more before the house and the country, for it is a very important subject. In my hurried glance over the debate on this subject last session I find that outside of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the then Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), none of the members on the other side expressed any opinion, with the exception of the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) and the then member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis). The latter opposed the resolution on constitutional grounds, and the member for Pontiac, while supporting the sentiment of the resolution, said he could not vote for it. The then Minister of Railways took the attitude that while he was very much impressed by the project, and rather believed in it sentimentally, he could not support it for various reasons. I was struck with the fact that this project, which probably is one of the most important before the people of this country to-day in some of its aspects-and I shall deal with a few of them very briefly before I sit down- dioes not receive the support apparently of anybody on the other side of the house. I noticed a moment ago that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) was in his seat, but he has since left the house. He comes from a section of the country where a national highway is felt to be a most desirable proposition because that part of northern Ontario is more or less isolated so far as motor highways are concerned, and I am surprised in view of the attitude of the people in Kenora and Fort Frances and the rest of the district with respect to this matter that the minister does not come out frankly in support of the resolution.

National Highways-Mr. Manion
The member for Athabaska in moving hia resolution stated that the proposed highway would cost in the neighbourhood of forty or fifty million dollars. I should like to remind him that several sections of road which could be used as parts of a national highway are already built. I admit that his figures are correct for the whole highway at a certain cost of construction per mile, but I think he will find that the sections of road already built in various parts of the Dominion could be incorporated in a national highway. I note that there are roads built through the western prairie provinces and through the mountains, and the roads through the national parks are being completed, as the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) said' a moment ago. But while the Prime Minister was at Calgary last autumn he was waited upon by a deputation in support of this very proposition, and the Minister of the Interior, who was with him at the time, is quoted in the Manitoba Free Press of November 19, as follows:
Hon. Charles Stewart, Minister of the Interior pointed out that the gosoline tax was bringing so much money that the provinces were not having the same difficulty in securing funds for road building as some years ago. The road between Kenora and Winnipeg would be opened within the next 18 months and he did not think more than 200 miles would be left for the province of Ontario to construct before the east would be linked -with the west.
I do not quite agree with the figures he gave:	I think there is more of the road to
be built across northern Ontario than he mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
More than
two hundred miles?

I think so. I take it to
be more than three hundred miles. I wish to give figures which I have made up roughly from estimates, as to what mileage really remains to be built. We can go from any part of eastern Canada to Sault Ste. Marie, the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Simpson) who made a very able speech favouring this proposition. But from the Soo to the Manitoba boundary there is a large gap-in fact it extends from the Soo to Winnipeg, because I do not think the Manitoba government has yet made contracts to build to the Ontario boundary, though the undertaking has been talked of a good deal. From the Soo to Chapleau I am informed on good authority that there is ninety miles of road already constructed; and from Nipigon to Fort William, a distance of sixty miles, taking it in a straight line, the road has been constructed; west of Fort William to Shebandowan there is another sixty miles of road, and then in the neighbourhood 2419-281
of the Minister of Labour's district, from Dry-den to Kenora, there is still another sixty miles of road. This means 270 miles of that gap has already been constructed. Taking the total distance from the Soo to the Manitoba boundary at six hundred miles, allowing for the curved manner in which, I take it, the road would run, we have a balance of about 330 miles yet to be constructed. This is, of course a rough estimate.
Not long ago I was with a deputation that waited on the provincial government of Ontario regarding unemployment, and the Minister of Lands and Forests stated in writing- it was published but I could not find it among my papers to-day-that the provincial government was quite willing to cooperate with this government in the building of that section of the highway extending across the gap of which we are speaking at the present moment.
There is this to remember regarding the building of national or provincial highways, that the provinces are in perhaps a rather difficult position to undertake alone the building of a straight national highway. Take, for instance, across the northern section of Ontario extending from Sudbury to the Manitoba boundary, in area nearly as large as Germany and France put together, with a population of only 200,000. This sparse population requires branch roads and a large amount of money is being expended in construction of branch colonization or settlers' roads. Therefore the provincial government should not be expected to build the whole of this proposed national highway across that section of northern Ontario. That after all is the only section remaining to link up these different roads which could be, for the time being at least, turned into a trans-Canada or a Canadian national highway. Therefore as I say, because of the demands upon the province, it is particularly necessary if the road is to be built that the Dominion government should take part in the work. The Dominion government should also take part in this road building from the national aspect of linking up the east with the west.
Now, regarding the cost of the road, I have taken the mileage at 330 miles. I noticed that last session the Prime Minister stated in discussing the resolution then before the house that the cost would run into something like $200,000,000, for a hard surfaced highway. Possibly it would, if the Dominion government undertook to put a hard surfaced highway across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but, as I think I can demonstrate, such a highway is not necessary or even desirable at the present time. All we require is a good

National Highways-Mr. Manion
gravel road. There are fine highways not only in Canada but in the United States of this construction, and they are very popular. I
have motored on quite a number of them myself in the sections south of Fort William and Duluth. Therefore I cannot agree with any such figures as $200,000,000 as representing the cost of completing a transcontinental highway. I think it is a figure simply put forward to discourage this proposed undertaking. Such an expenditure is not necessary at the present time.
But the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson), the Ontario whip, I think it was, made a speech recently, or at least he was quoted in one of the Toronto papers as saying, that the building of this road would cost something in the neighbourhood of four or five hundred million dollars, so that he went a little further than the Prime Minister did. Evidently he was thinking at that time that if he put up a high enough figure it would scare everybody away from it. However, I made it my business to look into some costs of different roads, and I ascertained from the Department of Railways itself, which has a highways branch, formed at the time my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) was in this house as a member of the government-
My hon. friend is wrong in that. The legislation was passed in 1919 for the highways aid, after I had left the government.

All right, I am wrong. I accept the hon. gentleman's statement in that. I did not wish to put him in wrong. I was simply quoting him, thinking he was another one of those who were taking a very broad view of the matter. However, I see he is taking rather a narrow view of it-
My hon. friend is presuming too much. He does not know yet what my point of view is.

I know very well what the hon. gentleman's point of view is. He is going to take the point of view that he is told to take, just as he has always done. He has always taken the point of view decided by the other side of the house even when he was sitting over on this side.
My hon. friend's imagination is running away with him.

Nothing of the kind. I was in the house at the same time the hon. gentleman was here. With regard to the cost of an ordinary gravel road, that was given to me as being an average of $11,000 a mile in

eastern Ontario. They also gave me figures for the building of roads in the Muskoka section, which is very much like the section in northern Ontario, rocky and more or less mountainous. The figure they gave me for a macadam road was $16,000 a mile, and for a water-tight macadam road $29,000. Taking the figures for the building of a road through the Muskoka section as being very much akin to the figures required to build a road through the northern Ontario section, I believe this road could be built for five or six million dollars. But supposing you doubled it, you would still have a figure which would be greatly below the figure given by the Prime Minister, and still more greatly below the figure given by the hon. member for South Perth. That is worth considering, five millions or six millions or seven millions, and if the Ontario government cooperates with the Dominion government in this matter then the cost to the Dominion government would only be half.
In addition to that, it has been suggested by some, although I do not know that I agree with it, that the road might be built through the clay belt, between the two railways, a distance of one hundred and fifty miles, where it would not cost any more than it would in eastern Ontario. I am personally of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that if the cost were not too great we could make a highway as picturesque as any highway in Europe by sticking as closely as we could to the north shore of lake Superior. You would then have a highway that would attract people from all over this continent.
I have noticed that when this matter has been up for discussion a great deal of the discussion has related to the question of the loss to the railways, although both Mr. Beatty and Sir Henry Thornton are authorities for the statement-I certainly saw Mr. Beatty quoted not so very long ago, and I think Sir Henry Thornton to the same effect-that although the automobile traffic has increased tremendously it has not decreased the earnings of the railways because of the freight and so forth that is given to the railways due to the development of the motor industry.
It might be added that there is no way of getting out of that northern Ontario section except by going through the United States, that is, by motor, after you pass Sault Ste. Marie. If you choose to go west from Sault Ste. Marie you must go across to the Michigan Soo, and if you wish to go by the head of the lakes you have to go via Duluth. And, by the way, that is merely a gravel highway, and the American side of it is largely gravel too. Last year, over that highway, there came into Fort William some thirteen

National Highways-Mr. Black (Yukon)
thousand cars with about fifty thousand tourists from the United States, an increase of something like twenty-five per cent over the previous year. Each year the number of automobile tourists coming in is rapidly increasing, and the tourist question, as has been well pointed out by previous speakers, is of the utmost importance to-day. In fact, it is a great national industry to-day. We have had various estimates from the Bureau of Statistics, and other departments, as to the amount of money spent in this Dominion by tourists last year, the amount given being anywhere from two hundred million to three hundred million dollars, and I thoroughly agree with the remarks made by my hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael), who quoted Mr. Neill, vice-president of the Royal Bank of Canada, as suggesting that we should do more advertising than we do in regard to that industry. Many of the countries of Europe to-day are spending vast sums of money in advertising, bringing tourists into their country-France, Italy, Germany, and even England-because tourist traffic means the spending of large amounts of money. When we built the Canadian Pacific railway many years ago we had hardly anybody living in the prairie provinces, and only a few thousand living west of the Rocky mountains. It required a great vision and great courage at that time to build that road through there, and I think that same vision and courage might well be brought into play at the present time by this government in regard to this national highway. It would bring about a better understanding, I think, between the east and the west. As has been said, it would give an opportunity for the people of the east to visit the west in their motor cars without going out of this country into the great republic to the south, and it would also afford an opportunity for those in the west to come east. It would also give a great impetus to those tourists coming from the United States to visit this country, because there is a desire on the part of most people who are touring in cars to go as far north as they can get. It would also afford a great opportunity for the people of the United States to make a complete tour, coming in at the east, around Niagara Falls, and going clean through to the west, even west of the head of the lakes into the prairie provinces.
There is something else in regard to this question which I think should have been considered by the government, and that very recently; that is, the need of having done something to assist the unemployed in the country. Many of the people who to-day are out of work in various parts of Canada
might well have been employed on such a project as this.
I submit in closing, Mr. Speaker, that in every way one may look at the matter, it seems to me it is a question well worthy of the support of this government, and well worthy of the support of this house, and I venture to make the assertion that if the government left the whole matter to the decision of the house, as most of these resolutions are left, it would be approved, perhaps not unanimously but very largely, by the vote of this chamber. And I submit, very seriously and sincerely, to the government, that they might well reconsider their attitude of last year-none of them have spoken on the question as yet to-day, and I am supposing their attitude is the same-and take the attitude that was taken by all those who spoke, with the exception of two last year, not including the members of the government, and support this project as a very strong Canadian project, and one which would be for the betterment of Canada in every possible way.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution is, in effect, a statement, that in the opinion of the house a substantial grant should be made to cover the development of highway construction, meaning, of course, national highway construction.
In that connection perhaps it would be fitting to direct the attention of the house to a highway project which is exciting great attention in western Canada and also in the western United States, and with which no doubt the Minister of the Interior is familiar. I refer to the continuation of the Pacific highway through British Columbia and the Yukon to Alaska, which would be typically a national highway. At present the highway extends from Mexico up through the states of California, Oregon and Washington almost to the northerly boundary of British Columbia. Thousands of tourists come over that highway every year to visit Canada, admire the scenery, enjoy our climate and spend their money. I am sure the government are very much in favour of encouraging tourist traffic in Canada, and I think no better contribution could be made along this line than a reasonable grant for the continuation of that highway. As I have said, the road has been built through British Columbia almost to the northern boundary; it is already constructed through Yukon territory and a comparatively small grant would be sufficient to put the highway in shape for tourist traffic. This project is being seriously considered by the government of British Columbia, and in this
438	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Black (Yukon)
connection I should like to read to the house the words of the premier of that province, as they appear in a despatch from Ottawa under date of September 9:
A grand plan for an international highway extending from the border of Mexico away up through British Columbia to the Yukon and Alaska was discussed at an interview here to-day between Premier Tolmie of British Columbia and Hon. Charles Stewart, Minister of the Interior. The provincial government is favourable to the plan, but it is of great magnitude, and federal aid will be necessary.
It is understood that Mr. Stewart was prepared to have the Dominion build the Yukon part of it	
That is very good news.
.... but did not commit himself on the other.
I presume that would be the section through British Columbia.
There are some 460 miles of new road in British Columbia, and about 125 miles in the Yukon required to carry out the scheme.
New construction in the Yukon will not total 125 miles, but a great many improvements will be necessary to the present roads to make them suitable for tourist traffic.
The lure of American tourists to the land of the midnight sun in Canada, just as Sw'eden and Norway in like latitudes are the great attraction of Europe, is the particular object of the plan.
Premier Tolmie explained that the highway would run from Tia Juana, Mexico, up the whole Pacific coast to the international boundary of British Columbia, connecting there with the roadway to Hazelton, B.C., and afterwards going on to connect with the Yukon and Alaska systems. "It would give United States people," he said, "an opportunity of visiting Alaska by road through the richest scenery in the world. It would give Canadians access to the Yukon -without going through the United States."
"It is a very large enterprise," Mr. Tolmie continued, "and our satisfactory talk to-day was necessarily of a general or preliminary character, but our Pacific coast people are deeply interested in this plan and we are very hopeful of it ultimately going through."
The matter has gone even further on the other side of the line; already a bill has been passed by the United States Senate and House of Representatives appropriating $25,000 for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did you say $25,000?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution
under discussion is very interesting to the members of this house and, I am sure, to every citizen of Canada. I have no quarrel with the desire to see a national highway across Canada, although my opinion may differ somewhat as to how that work should be done, so I have very little comment to make on much of what has been said this afternoon. However, I must say that most of the speakers who have addressed the house appear to be of the opinion that the federal govern-

National Highways-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
meat is doing nothing in the way of highway construction or for the purpose of attracting tourist traffic, and I am afraid I cannot agree with those statements.
I was greatly relieved to learn that such a small portion of a national transcontinental highway remains to be constructed; I was under the impression that a very much larger mileage remained. From the remarks which have been made this afternoon I think we may assume that we have a fairly good highway from the Atlantic coast to Sault Ste. Marie in Ontario. I do not think that can be denied, nor do I think any hon. member will advocate any large expenditure on that portion of the highway, which reaches almost half way across Canada. Then we had the statement by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) that the government of Saskatchewan is to undertake the construction of three highways across that province, and he expressed the fear that they might not connect with the highways constructed in Manitoba and Alberta. I can iteassure my hon. friend on that point; I took the precaution to examine the routes suggested by the government of Saskatchewan, and those highways will connect at two points with the highways in Alberta.
I would not make the statement that in the southern part of Alberta there are allweather highways, but I understand that the provincial government intend to have an allweather highway across that province at the earliest possible moment, running from Medicine Hat to Calgary and on to the entrance to the Banff section, this being the first part of a national highway leading from the prairie provinces to the coast. In addition, I know the provincial government of Alberta has been extending the highway from Edmonton eastward, and undoubtedly it will soon reach the town of Lloydminster. Then we will have three highways leading across that province; these may not be all-weather highways, but they will be gravel highways of a fairly good type.
So I think we may assume that one would have very little difficulty at present in travelling from Winnipeg to the Rocky mountains with an automobile at any season of the year, except perhaps in the middle of winter. I believe there remains about forty miles of highway to be constructed in the eastern portion of Manitoba to reach the boundary and connect with the highway presently under construction from Kenora, so really the serious obstacle to an all-Canadian highway at present is the stretch between Sault Ste. Marie and the Manitoba boundary, across which there are roads at broken intervals.
I think I am correct in saying that the provincial government of Ontario has made very rapid progress in the construction of this highway. They have spent annually considerable sums of money upon it, and I think it would not be beyond the bounds of possibility to say that within two years that highway will be entirely completed. At such time the break will be complete, with the exception of the portion which I will deal with later. That section is in the Rocky mountains connecting British Columbia with the prairies.
Now, may I say in passing that I do not wish it to be inferred that the federal government is seeking to avoid responsibility. I must say, however, that I do not think it is the work of the federal government to assist in the construction of these highways. My hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) has stated that we are obligated to assist in the construction of highways because we collect the sum of $27,000,000 by way of tariff through the importation of automobiles into this country. May I remind the hon. member that we collect a great deal of revenue on importations into Canada of various products, and automobiles is only one of them. But every hon. member in this house must agree that the expenditure by the federal government has been tremendously increased. I have no doubt that the $27,000,000 my hon. friend mentioned will, in a very considerable degree, be required for the increased payments to our returned men, when the committee which has to deal with pensions and returned soldier matters has completed its inquiry and made a report to this house. That is only one example of where we may be called upon to make increased expenditures; in every direction increases in expenditure are required by this parliament. Without tiring the house by repeatedly referring to the act of confederation, I have no doubt my hon. friend will admit that the duties of the federal parliament were fairly well defined under that act. No hon. gentleman will contend that the construction of highways was one of the duties that devolved upon the federal government.
Do hon. gentlemen opposite take into consideration the fact that this government is called upon time and again to support the construction of railways into the newer sections of Canada? Year by year such construction is required, more especially in connection with the Canadian National railway system, and no one will contend that this construction is self supporting. The taxpayers of Canada must make their contribution until such times as these newly opened territories are in condition to maintain the railway and pay for the portion of maintenance chargeable to them.
440	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
That is a duty that has devolved upon the federal government. It has been contended very frequently by members sitting on the opposite side of this house, that a large sum of unpaid balances of this Canadian National railway system is piling up, year by year, which will have to be taken care of by the taxpayers of this country. I think we should consider the demands that are made upon the federal treasury for expenditures which belong rightfully to this government.
It is the easiest thing in the world to pass a resolution saying that the federal government should bear the responsibility for this or that particular service. Such resolutions sometimes go to the extent of encroaching upon the duties of the provincial governments. May I say to the hon. gentlemen opposite that the federal government, no matter who may be holding the reins of office, will find that there are plenty of demands upon the revenues of the country, without the government taking upon itself responsibilities of a purely provincial nature. May I say that I agree most thoroughly with the statement of my leader that if the provinces require assistance they may get it in the way it has been given to the maritimes and the western provinces. They may get it by the return of their natural resources, and the absolute control of their own money to spend in whatever way they deem best. They would not receive it by way of grants for this service or that service which from time to time may be suggested by some enthusiastic organization such as the Automobile Association of Canada, although we must admit such associations as this launch propaganda for worthy projects.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have been doing something towards the construction of highways in Canada; we are doing something today. We have built a highway through the national parks at Banff, Yoho and Kootenay that will be a connecting link between the west coast and the prairie provinces, and will complete the Rocky mountain section of a trans-Canada highway. We are spending very considerable sums upon that highway, and not only that, but we have spent a very considerable sum to make accessible and improve the scenic values of Banff national park, in order to encourage tourist traffic.

How much has been
spent, do you know?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am unable to give the figures this afternoon. We have spent on the highway in the Rocky mountains in the neighbourhood of $718,000 up to date. Of that highway which consists of 195 miles, 
from Revelstoke to Golden, 157 miles remain to be constructed. Part of that highway should have gone rightfully across Glacier park. Owing, however, to the conditions that prevail there and the short season the highway would be open, we deemed it wise not to construct through Glacier park, but to cooperate with the province of British Columbia in building from Golden to Revelstoke, via the big bend. On this route wre are spending the amount which it would have cost to construct a highway across Glacier Park. We are contributing that amount on the stretch of 195 miles and are constructing our portion on the eastern end of the gap under the supervision of our own engineers. This is the last link in the highway between the prairies and the coast.

How much does it cost
per mile?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am unable to say. We simply agreed that our share of construction was $850,000, and that is the estimated amount that would have been required to construct the highway across Glacier park. We are in no way joining the provincial government; we are simply making a contribution of the amount it would have cost us to pass through the territory controlled and administered by the federal government.

Is part of it not being
built by the federal government, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We are expending the whole $850,000 under our own supervision.

Who will take care of
the upkeep of the road, after it is built?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The provincial government will take care of the upkeep of that particular piece of road. We of course maintain the roads in our own park.

The British Columbia
government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The British Columbia government will maintain the area outside of the park.
In connection with the tourist traffic I agree with what the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) has to say. I would be very glad to get larger appropriations for advertising for tourist traffic, but I do want to point out that for some years we have been advertising thoroughly in every state of the union, through the natural resources intelligence branch of this department, getting out maps and indicating the roads available, the scenic attractions of the various com-

National Highways-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
munities and sending with that material literature prepared by the provincial government, and in this way getting the information to the automobile, tourist associations and all other associations of that character. I am pleased to say that the tourist traffic of Canada has increased very rapidly from $90,000,000 or more until it is estimated that last year it amounted to well over $300,000,000.
In connection with the tourist business, the provincial governments receive a very substantial benefit. They have a tax upon all the gasoline consumed and, moreover, on all the tourist cars that come into our country as well as cars that come from other directions and travel over the 500 odd miles of park highway that we have constructed, they get without cost to themselves the same revenue that they receive in respect to their own particular highways. As a federal government we get nothing in return for this expenditure. I have on more than one occasion stated that the federal government stands prepared to take over the necessary territory to create a national park in every province in Canada. Just recently we have retained a territory in Saskatchewan and in the negotiations with Manitoba we have retained in that province a territory which we will develop as a national park. All these places will be made as attractive as possible to encourage tourist traffic to come to Canada. All the facilities, roads, and everything else in those parts are, so far as the federal government is concerned, free to the public; the federal government will derive no revenue therefrom.
There is a licence fee in some cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A mere registration fee on entering the park, for the purpose of keeping track of the people going in and out. That is all the direct motor traffic revenue we get out of the park. That service is maintained for the purpose of encouraging tourist traffic, which no one will deny is very important to this country. As I said before, we stand ready and willing to give those facilities to every province which is desirous of having them, provided we are given the territory free of charge.
In Saskatchewan the creation of a park and the provision of necessary facilities has meant an expenditure so far of something like $200,000, and it will amount to practically $500,000 before we get through with it. Possibly one could estimate the establishment of a park in each one of those provinces at something like half a million dollars, and then there is the annual upkeep which is bound to be more or less expensive as the years go by. Moreover, there are bound to be greater and greater demands for park facilities.
With respect to the statement made by the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Black), the Premier of British Columbia was here some time ago, and was quite enthusiastic about a coast highway through British Columbia and on to Alaska through the Yukon. My hon. friend is quite correct. I at once agreed, on behalf of the federal government, that so far as the Yukon territory was concerned, if that project was to be gone on with, we would be quite willing to build our share of the highway just as we are willing to build our share of highways through the national parks. I was not aware that anything in the nature of a survey was being attempted, although I was given to understand that possibly the British Columbia government would confirm the survey from the Portland canal to the boundary of the Yukon. So far I have not heard whether or not that is the intention of the British Columbia government, but as I say, the federal government is willing to construct what I consider our share of the highway in its entirety across the Yukon, in order not to block the construction of a highway that the people of the west coast think so desirable.
With respect to the other request of the Premier of British Columbia that financial assistance be given, I was unable to speak because that is a matter of policy which would have to be considered by the federal government.
In conclusion, I think the federal government is making a very substantial contribution towards a national highway. I made the statement to the province of Alberta some years ago, when they were considering a highway through Jasper park to connect with what was then the proposed highway to Vancouver, that they would not need to delay for the territory occupied by the Jasper national park. We could, within the space of one year, complete all the highway within the park area, but so far the provincial government have not reached the boundary of Jasper national park. I believe they intend to do so this year and then it will be necessary to build on through Jasper and connect with the highway going on down to Vancouver and, possibly later on, to Prince Rupert. We are providing these facalities; we are doing this advertising in the United States and elsewhere to bring tourists to Canada. We are prepared to provide the scenic attraction in national parks in every province; we are prepared to build and maintain the highways in those parks and give those facilities to the

National Highways-Mr. Guthrie
public practically free of charge. This, in my opinion, is no small contribution to the resolution moved by my hon. friend that the federal government .contribute to a national highway.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for
Fort William (Mr. Manion) was addressing you in regard to this motion, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) interjected a remark which did not agree with my recollection of a matter which took place in the year 1919 when the house passed a bill known as the Highways Act. I gathered from what the Minister of Railways said this afternoon when he interrupted the hon. member for Fort William that he would have the house believe that he was not a party to the legislation which the house passed in the session of 1919. That is not my recollection of the matter, and I think my recollection is correct, and that of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways is astray.
In the year 1919 I happened to be, in a humble capacity, a member of 'the government of Sir Robert Borden, as was also my hon. friend the present Minister of Railways. We introduced into the house, on the 21st of March of that year, the Highways Act. That act represented the policy of the government of that time. It was, of course, preceded by a resolution and I have given the date upon which the resolution was introduced into this chamber. The present Minister of Railways was certainly a member of the government of that day. The resolution was passed; the bill received its first and, I think likely, its second reading. On the 4th of June my hon. friend the present Minister of Railways tendered his resignation to Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister of Canada. On the following day, or perhaps the same day, the resignation was read in the house. It is true that the bill was not finally assented to until the 7th of July, but when the policy was adopted by the government as a whole, the Minister of Railways was a party to it and approved it.
When he resigned from the government, he did not resign on account of the highways bill. He was very specific: he resigned on account of the fiscal policy of the government of that day. He was present as a supporter and member of the government when the bill was introduced and the resolutions were carried. He was part and parcel of the administration and must accept his full responsibility for the legislation which was then passed. I also 
was a supporter of the government. I am not going to go into the question now before the chair, more than to say that I too am a supporter of the present resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext: My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has brought up some rather ancient history. If my recollection serves me, my hon. friend was not a member of the Union government during the period that I was a member of it.
Oh yes, I was.
My hon. friend was Solicitor General.
I was a member of the government just the same. Perhaps if my hon. friend knew the situation a little better he would not make that statement.
My hon. friend was not in the cabinet at that time.
I did not say that I was in the cabinet.
Then my hon. friend does not know what took place in the cabinet in reference to the highways 'bill.
I was Solicitor General in that government.
My hon. friend is quibbling.
Oh, oh.
Order.

My recollection of the
matter is veiy distinct. It is quite true that this legislation was introduced into the house prior to my resigning from the government. The reason the legislation was introduced at that time was that there were probably
500,000	soldiers presently to be demobilized.
It is well to go back to the beginning of this highways legislation so far as this parliament is concerned. Legislation was first introduced in 1912, after the elelotion of 1911. During that election the then leader of the Conservative party, Sir Robert Borden, made some statements of policy, so far as his party was concerned, in respect to the matter of federal assistance to highways should his party be returned. The legislation was introduced in 1912. There was a difference of opinion with that other chamber which is part of the legislative machinery of this country as to the terms of the legislation. The matter was then left in abeyance until 1913, when it was again brought up, but no further progress was made before the outbreak of war. During

National Highways-Mr. Crerar
the war the matter again remained in abeyance, but at its conclusion it was brought up again, not on the principle, as stated in the resolution before the house, that it was recognized that the federal parliament should make a contribution towards highway construction, but in recognition of the fact that there were
500,000	soldiers to be demobilized, and it was necessary to provide some form of employment for their reabsorption into some useful industry.
Coming to the resolution before the house, the preamble reads:
Whereas the need for establishment of highways is greater than in 1919;
That is given as one of the reasons why action as suggested in the concluding paragraph of the resolution should be taken by the federal government, but, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the need for highways is as great now as it was in 1919. Since that time all the provinces of Canada have been spending very large sums of money indeed on highway construction.
