The second paragraph of the resolution states that there was a definite recognition by the federal government in 1919 of its responsibility in the matter of highways. That is not my recollection. Let me say again that the chief reason, as I recall, for making the grant at that time was in order to assist in the reestablishment of the demobilized soldiers by providing some form of employment for them. This assistance was given to the provinces at that time largely for that purpose, and the assistance was extended' for several years until the amount of $20,000,000 provided for by the legislation had been granted to the provincial authorities.
I do not know that I can add very much to what my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has said in regard to this resolution. I think it was recognized at the commencement of our confederation pact that so far as the federal authority was concerned, it was responsible for railway transportation, and responsible for the very important and onerous duty of improving the harbours and rivers of this country for the purposes of navigation. From that earliest period of confederation down to the time when $20,000,000 was granted by the federal government in 1919 for highway construction, the principle had never been advocated that the federal authority was responsible in any degree for the building or maintenance of highways. The federal authority has assumed the responsibility of railway construction, and the responsibility of improving our harbours and rivers, and its obligations in those respects
have been very onerous and heavy indeed. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has referred to our obligations in connection with the national railways. They are very heavy, and I am afraid are bound to continue heavy for several years to come. We are developing an outlet, for instance, to the Hudson bay. We are improving the navigation on the St. Lawrence river. The federal authority has built the Welland canal. On all these projects the federal government has spent in the last twenty years, not scores of millions, but hundreds of millions of dollars, and if there is to be any fair basis for distributing the cost of all these works, I submit that you cannot fairly impose on the federal authority the burden, or any part of it, of also building provincial highways. I recognize, of course, that it is a first-class talking point for hon. gentlemen opposite, but, after all, we must have some regard for the financial position of Canada, and for the country's financial obligations. Before the war it was a wholly different matter. Our debt then was a comparatively trivial thing and our national revenue needs were comparatively trivial; but the war added two billions of dollars to our national debt, with its burden of interest, and added forty million dollars a year for pensions. As the Minister of the Interior has intimated, there is not the slightest doubt that when the report is brought down by the pensions committee this session, our obligation in respect to pensions will be still further increased, and quite properly so.
That being the case, I submit that it is not reasonable, in view of all the assistance which it is giving at the present time in building and maintaining highways in national parks, to expect the federal government to saddle itself with this additional expenditure. We must have some regard to the taxpaying capacity of the Canadian people, and I submit that if my hon. friends opposite would have some regard for that phase of the question, they would perhaps not be so insistent in urging this expenditure as they have been this afternoon.

I should like to give one or two reasons why the government should not hesitate to support this resolution. The history of our roads is one of the most fascinating and instructive stories in Canada's development. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec, the cities of Montreal, Toronto, Kingston, and the ancient city of Quebec, primarily owe their great development to the roads that were inaugurated in the early years of Canada's history. We find' likewise that England's great industrial develop-
National Highways-Mr. Brady

ment was due in a large part to her splendid system of roads. All European countries are to-day paying more and more attention to improving and extending their systems of public highways. That being the case, it seems to me strange to hear from the government benches opposition to this resolution, and arguments which are unconvincing because of the fact that they are not in accord with the practical development of Canada at this time and period.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I read with deep interest the story of the Canada Highways Act when it was first placed on the statute books, in 1919, and this is the first time I have heard that there was a secondary reason for granting $20,000,000 for the development and improvement of a highway system throughout the Dominion. I am sure that no member of this house, and certainly no one outside the house, will say that that expenditure did not help forward the progress of Canada by leaps and bounds. The result of the non-continuance of federal aid to highways is that those parts of Canada, particularly western and mid-Canada, are to-day sorely handicapped regarding road construction, and are, in consequence, the only provinces that in recent years that have failed to keep pace with the other portions of Canada. In view of this, sir, I wonder if the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) really conscientiously believes that the preamble of this resolution is not in accordance with the facts.
He denies that the need for the establishment of highways is greater to-day than it was in 1919. I submit, sir, that the need for highways is necessarily greater to-day than it was in 1919. What do we find to-day? On all sides of this house we find cumulative evidence of the fact that the great need of Canada to-day is roads, and more roads. There has been a marvellous increase in our tourist trade, and an equally marvellous increase in the number of Canadian owned automobiles and motor busses. Furthermore, there are wonderful opportunities in western Canada for a farsighted policy on the part of our government which would develop the tremendous wealth lying there. Any governmental expenditure made to encourage that development will come back tenfold, as will any federal expenditure which we are asking towards the completion of this portion of our national highways.
The point I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, is that we are asking for something which we believe will result in the better development of Canada as a whole. When the Canada Highways Act was in operation, $80,-

000	was granted each province over a five year period, and the balance was distributed in proportion to population. Since that money was spent British Columbia-which to my mind presents the greatest road problem of any of our provinces-is being forced to develop, for the interest, of the Dominion government as much as for the province, this immense undertaking. I should like you, Mr. Speaker, to picture for one moment the situation of the city that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) said he hoped would very soon be linked up with our transcontinental highway. I refer to Prince Rupert. Do you know, sir, that to-day we have not a road linking uip that city with any other city or town in Canada? Only ninety miles of road construction from the port of Prince Rupert would bring us in touch with our Canadian highway and enable the people of that city to travel to Vancouver or eastern Canada. Now, what would that road cost?
1	believe it will be a costly undertaking, but it is going to open up one of the finest scenic sections, n-ot merely of British Columbia but of any part of the Dominion. I refer to that wonderful stretch of river and mountain scenery between Prince Rupert and Terrace, a distance of ninety miles.
Is it possible we do not know that in the last ten years public opinion in Canada has changed with regard to our highways? Changed conditions bring about a new set of facts that we must face squarely. What are these facts? We are in a great machine age, the most marvellous period of development in any past era. We demand these highways for our own national development. It is not a mere petty local demand; we are making the demand looking at Canada as a whole. True, we have our railways, but they can do for the development of the country exactly what they are intended to do and nothing more. They are intended for transportation purposes, for colonization purposes, and as great avenues for the transportation of freight and passengers. But, sir, what about our roads? Roads to-day are part of our modern civilization. They are for the use, not of the wealthy alone but of all the people; and if we do not get a sufficient program of road building put into effect, I want to tell you that you to a great extent are stopping the natural progress and development of the very country that is willing to return, to you far more than you can give it.
I do not want to labour this point, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to say anything hypercritical regarding the action of the government. But let me point out that there

National Highways-Mr. Kaiser
is not any city, town or village in Canada where you will not find public bodies pledged to the continued development of the highways of Canada. Is not that public opinion? We cannot excuse ourselves on the plea that the federal government is spending money indirectly for purposes in respect to which we are asking it to spend directly. We know that the federal government is spending money, but that is merely avoiding the issue. Reference has been made to members of the government "trotting out," as it was described, the "old British North America Act." I do not think, Mr. Speaker, we should speak disparagingly of that enactment. After all, it sets out first what are our constitutional responsibilities in this parliament, and, second, what are the constitutional responsibilities of the provincial legislatures. This resolution does not call upon us to discharge what is a federal constitutional responsibility. This parliament and previous parliaments have discharged continuously the constitutional responsibility of the Dominion in regard to transportation. With respect to water transportation, the Dominion to-day is carrying practically the whole of the load of providing such facilities; harbours, rivers, our great canal systems-all are wholly Dominion responsibilities. The Dominion is carrying its constitutional load with respect to railway transportation. In fact the Dominion is now discharging obligations annually which were originally assumed by the provinces with respect to railways. In many of the provinces, Mr. Speaker, the provincial governments assumed, for reasons which seemed good to themselves at the time, the responsibility of guaranteeing the bonds of railway companies provincially incorporated for the purpose of building railways wholly within the borders of the province. With the exception of two railways, one in British Columbia and the other in Ontario, the Dominion is to-day 
discharging whatever responsibilities attach to these provincial guarantees, and they amount to a very considerable sum. I have not the figures under my hand, but I do not t.hin.lr that $100,000,000 in capital expenditure is stating too much in regard to the provincial transportation guarantees which to-day are being discharged by the federal authority instead of by the provincial governments which originally gave them. Then the Dominion is called upon to assume a responsibility to-day in connection with a new form of transportation-aerial transportation. Who will deny that the backbone of aerial transportation in Canada to-day is the air mail system which is being developed by the Dominion government? Through the contracts which are being let from time to time by the Postmaster General, regular air mail routes are established and are used by the general public of Canada for the carriage of passengers and freight. In that regard the provinces are assuming at the present time no financial responsibility.
That, then, is our constitutional responsibility, and we are discharging it. What we are asked,' as a Dominion parliament, by a resolution such as this is to do as a matter of grace what we are not constitutionally obligated to do-as a matter of grace to make grants to the provinces in order that they may be the better able to discharge their constitutional responsibilities. The framers of the British North America Act did not contemplate grants being made systematically as a matter of grace. I opposed the system of making grants as a matter of grace when I was a provincial minister, and I take the same attitude to-day. I take the attitude that the fields of taxation are delimited as between the federal and provincial authorities; their obligations are broadly delimited also, and if the provinces find themselves unable to exploit reasonably as they may their fields of taxation to carry out the constitutional obligations imposed upon them, then it is the business of the Dominion and of the provinces in conference assembled to consider whether or not the free subsidies now granted-as a matter of the constitution, not as a matter of grace-by this parliament to the provinces should be increased.
Why do I say that? Not only from the point of view of protecting the federal treasury, Mr. Speaker-that is not the allimportant thing-but as a matter of safeguarding the autonomy of the provinces themselves. I speak from experience as a provincial minister. Others in this house on both sides have had the experience of de-

National Highways-Mr. Dunning
bating this matter from the point of view of the provinces in the various legislatures. The Dominion comes along to a province and says: As a matter of grace we are prepared to vote to you a certain sum of money for a certain period of years, provided you do such and so. That is a distinct invitation to the province; indeed, it is often a monetary consideration to the province to embark upon a policy which otherwise the province might not consider itself able to undertake at the time. That was the case as a matter of fact with the province of Alberta at the time the Dominion Highways Act was first enacted. It did not feel itself in a position to take advantage of that legislation, it did not feel it could afford to raise the sum of money necessary to put up the sixty per cent of the total amount provided for by the act, and for a number of years not only that province, but other provinces did not find it possible to avail themselves of the act, and as a matter of fact its terms had to be extended from year to year over a period of yeans beyond the original term, in order that the .provinces might be able to take up the quota prescribed for them.
The same, Mr. Speaker, its true with respect to others of these grants which have been made as a matter of grace. I am of the opinion that if that principle were continued and expanded, as it could be from time to time, it would lead to a centralization of governmental and parliamentary authority which is distinctly not contemplated by our constitution. If there is need for further grants from this Dominion to the provinces, I submit, sir, there is a constitutional way to do it, and that way is by gathering the provinces together and subsequently this parliament deciding to suggest to the imperial parliament an amendment to the constitution -as has in fact been done on previous occasions-enlarging the amount paid by the Dominion to the provinces. This parliament imposes no conditions that any part of the moneys so granted shall be spent for highways, for technical education, or for this or that purpose; the subsidies paid leave the provinces entirely free to control their own policies in their own legislatures as contemplated by the constitution.

Others want it to be wide enough to enable grants to be made to the provinces to build main market roads.

I think, Mr. Speaker, it is the obligation of hon. members of this house when they bring forward resolutions of this kind, imposing as they would, if implemented, a load upon the Dominion treasury, to tell the house the amount of financial obligation involved in carrying into effect the terms of the resolution proposed. Ontario is the province which has been referred to by a number of the speakers as having within its borders the gap which at present prevents continuous travel by road from eastern Canada to western Canada.
And the province of Manitoba, partly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and a little in the province of Manitoba, which I understand is already arranged for by the province of Manitoba. However that may be, the province of Ontario is, without doubt, the wealthiest province in the Dominion. The surplus reported a few days ago by that province does not indicate that it is in any need of grants by grace from this parliament in order to enable it to discharge its constitutional obligations. I would also point out to my hon. friends from Nova Scotia and Alberta who spoke to this resolution that they did not discuss, or name in their resolution, the basis upon which division should be made of any moneys which might be voted, by grace, by this parliament. It will be remembered that in the former case the moneys were voted to be granted to the provinces on the basis of population. The province which had the most people, got the most money, and the province which got the most money has still the biggest gap in any national highway system. That is not a criticism of the province of Ontario. They used the money in those parts of the province where it was most needed and where their people were. That is a very natural thing. But I would like my hon. friends from the province of Alberta and the province of Nova Scotia to express some views as to the principle which should be followed in dividing such moneys among the provinces if they were granted. These questions I have endeavoured to raise are all questions-

Last year
members from Alberta, on this side of the house at least, made it quite clear in the debate that took place then that they considered the mileage basis to be the fairest way of distributing the amount of a grant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, in
answer to that I can venture the assertion

National Highways-Mr. Adshead
that had it been based upon mileage in the resolution there would not be the apparently unanimous support for it which now obtains on the other side of the house-
Speak for yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-any more than there would be unanimous support for a resolution which called merely for a national highway.
Hon. members, in addressing the house, have made it very clear as to what they desire. Some have asked for a national highway, others for grants to provinces to enable them to build main market roads. I suppose hon. members-

Is the hon. gentleman
cognizant- of the plans of the United States and how the money is divided there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I think I am fairly cognisant of their plan. Is my hon. friend advocating a United States system of dealing with this highway?
So far as federal grants are concerned, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, there is another
opinion slightly different from some that we have heard this afternoon.
I cannot vote for this resolution, first, because of what I have previously stated; second, because the movers of it and those speaking in support of it do not indicate what the financial load shall be upon the Dominion, nor do they indicate in the resolution any principle upon which division should be made between the provinces which are to be served by it; and, finally, because I believe this Dominion has at the present time, in connection with water transportation and air transportation, with its tremendous responsibility with respect to railway transportation, with the need that exists for progressively reducing her public debt and reducing taxation, plenty to take care of without going, by grace, into the field of provincial responsibility and handing out money to another authority for a purpose which is really their own.

I
had not intended to speak on this resolution, but the speeches of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) and the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) compel me to make a point or two with regard to the prairie provinces.
The hon. member for Pictou made special reference to the claims of the province of Nova Scotia. In that regard may I impress upon the Minister of Finance, whom I am sorry to see leaving the chamber, that the
prairie provinces occupy a position distinctly different from that occupied to-day by the provinces of eastern Canada. The eastern provinces always have had their own natural resources; Ontario has drawn great revenues from its timber limits, its mines and other natural resources, so Ontario has been better able to provide for those matters which are under the control of the provinces only. The minister said we were asking for an act of grace. As far as the province of Alberta is concerned we are not asking for anything as an act of grace; we are simply asking for an act of justice. The provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have not had their natural resources; they have received no revenue from mines, timber limits, oil leases or licences, or other matters of that kind. The revenue from those sources has gone to the Dominion government, and the province of Alberta has been crippled because of that fact.
How long have the prairie provinces been waiting for those -resources;? We have been waiting since 1911, and probably longer than that. I heard Sir Robert Borden state in tiie city of Calgary that the Conservative government would not be in office twenty-four hours before the natural resources would be returned to Alberta. Eighteen years have passed, during which time all the revenues have been going to the federal treasury, and because of that loss of revenue we are compelled to ask the Dominion government to help us along these lines. Go back to 1911, when those natural resources were promised. Ever since that time they have been a political football, pushed from one party to the other for various reasons until this year, and as yet we have had no revenue from them; as yet nothing has come into the province of Alberta whereby she could fulfil her obligations with respect to roads and technical education. Take the amount paid the Dominion government for oil licences, mining licences, timber licences and so on from 1911 to the present time; hand that amount to the province of Alberta and we will not ask this government to perform an act of grace. All we are asking is an act of justice. So far as the prairie provinces are concerned, because we are not on the same footing as the rest of the provinces which have had their resources from which they have received great revenues, we ask as an act of justice that the prairie provinces should be granted the aid necessary to provide for the construction of roads and for technical education.
Mr. ,T. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre): I should like to add a word of protest in regard to the attitude of the Minister
454	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Woodsworth
of Finance towards the British North America Act. He objected to it having been trotted out. I am sorry he is behind the curtains, but he can hear what I have to say. His speech was a splendid example of the way in which the British North America Act is being used almost daily in this house. He spoke of the constitutional responsibility of this government and went on to say that they were responsible for the air routes. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance to name the clause in the British North America Act which gives the Dominion parliament control over the air routes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend had listened to me he would have heard that we have a constitutional responsibility with respect to mail, and that air mail is the backbone of air transportation. That is the very phrase I used.

I heard that. We have a responsibility with regard to mails, but we have no responsibility at all with regard to air transportation. One of these days mail may be carried largely by truck, I suppose. The trucks will have to be run over highways, and when that is done, for the life of me I do not know how truck-carried mail is less a federal responsibility than air mail.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may point out to my hon. friend that to-day mails do travel in that way, and they are subsidized by the Dominion because it is a Dominion rseponsibility.

How can they travel unless there are roads upon which they may run? How can they operate in bad weather unless there are hard surfaced roads? The minister cannot avoid the question in that way. The fact is that there is no provision whatsoever in the British North America Act in regard to air communication; there is not one word that says the Dominion government is responsible for air communication. I think it natural that we should assume such to be the case, but it is not in the British North America Act. Further than that, the automobile had not been invented when the British North America Act was drawn up, and the ordinary means of rapid communication between provinces at that time was either by steamship or railway line. Naturally those methods of communication which were not merely local in character, but which connected province with province and had communication with other parts of the world, were to be under Dominion jurisdiction.
I think that is very clear, if you read the British North America Act itself. Take for 'W Woodsworth.]
example subsection 10 of clause 92, which defines the work of the provincial legislatures. The clause reads:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:
(a) Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province.
The very idea there was that if there were means of communication between the provinces or extending beyond the provinces to any other country, they should be under federal jurisdiction. It seems to me that Since we are now using automobiles, more or less, instead of and in competition with the railways, when automobile roads run between the provinces, or come up from the United States to carry tourist traffic, as we have been told to-day, essentially those roads are not local or provincial in character, but they affect the welfare of the whole Dominion. I do not think it is an extravagant proposal that the Dominion should make some provision for helping out the provinces in matters of this kind. However I am not speaking so much in support of the resolution itself as I am protesting against the use of the British North America Act which w'as made once more tonight, as it is being made every day, absolutely ignoring the circumstances under which the British North America Act was drafted and presuming that we to-day are not ourselves to adopt those measures which are so sorely needed to meet the needs of the present day.

In looking at this resolution I find that it is somewhat general, but following the discussion to-day it would seem that a very great deal of attention had been paid to a national highway across Canada. I think the discussion has centered largely upon that point. Probably the intention of the resolution was not so much that alone as that a grant should be given to each of the provinces. So far as a national highway is concerned, I am in favour of it; I feel that we in the east, and our friends in the west, should not be compelled to take off our hats to the officials of a foreign country in order that we may get from one side of our country to the other. The assistance which was given formerly to the provinces by this government, especially to the smaller provinces in the eastern part of our Dominion, was of great help to them. Those provinces have not the same resources and the same means of increasing revenue as have the central and larger provinces, and so far as Nova Scotia is concerned the burden placed upon

National Highways-Mr. Black (Halifax)
that province with its limited revenue is almost staggering. As the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) has stated to-night, one-half of the revenue of that province is applied to roads. That is a very severe tax and one which curtails allotment and assistance to very important matters within the province. For instance, education, technical and otherwise; health; hospitals, general and special, all require assistance and it is not within the power of the provincial government to fulfil the needs of those various institutions. There are many other things which are in the public interest and which should be helped and supported, but there is not sufficient revenue with which to do it.
The Minister of Highways in Nova Scotia has stated that during the.next twenty years the expenditure in connection with the provincial highways would probably reach the huge sum of $90,000,000. That would mean about $4,500,000 annually for upkeep, an amount which I do not think the province of Nova Scotia can expend. Our trunk roads possibly may be maintained in the state of efficiency in which they now are, but no money will be available for the by-roads or secondary roads and no progress will be made in putting them in such shape as present day conditions warrant. I think it was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) who complained that we have made no suggestions as to how this money should be divided and how it shall be expended, and so on; it is up to the government to present its proposal which in due and proper time can be fully discussed.
I will add only that I intend to support this resolution with the hope that a generous al- [DOT] lotment may be given to Nova Scotia and to the maritime provinces.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution is
similar to the one brought before the house last year. At that time I had some reasons for opposing the resolution, and nothing has happened to cause me to change my mind in that regard.
When matters like this come before parliament we must find out if we have the power to act, then if according to the constitution of this country this parliament has a right to act, it can do so. Section 92 of the British North America Act, which deals with the exclusive powers of the provincial legislatures, reads as follows:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
8.	Municipal institutions in the province.
The provincial acts relating to roads and highways are almost identical in each of the provinces. There are local and county roads, which come under the jurisdiction of the local and county municipalities. Within the past few years that policy has been changed by some legislatures so that the province itself may take care of some of the highways previously under the control of the local or county authorities. That change was rightly made, because according to the constitution of this country the matter was within the jurisdiction of the province. The province could have the control of the different roads placed under whatever jurfsdiction they wished, provided it dealt with provincial roads only. As has been so ably explained by other hon. members during the course of this debate, the first step taken by this government in this direction was in 1919, long after confederation, when it was desired to give some work to the veterans who had just been discharged from the army.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is not within the scope of this House of Commons or of this parliament to deal with the matter suggested by the proposer of this resolution (Mr. Kellner). I believe that if parliament took the step suggested by the hon. member, such a step would be unconstitutional, we would have no right to take it, because the constitution which gives us the powers we have does not grant the power to do what is required or suggested by the resolution. It would be a very desirable thing indeed to have an interprovincial or national highway running from Halifax to Vancouver, but it should be done by those empowered by the law to do it.
It is very easy to travel by highway through Canada from Winnipeg to Vancouver and from Port Arthur to Halifax. The only portion at present unbuilt is the lake Superior section, comprising about 600 miles in northern Ontario. I believe the best policy for road construction is to build roads where there are people living. This is a long stretch of rocky, mountainous country, where no one lives. It would take an enormous sum of money to build a highway through that country, and it would be very upleasant to motor such a long distance without any hotel accommodation.
I believe, also, as the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. McKenzie) has said, the provinces at present have better revenues than they had formerly. For instance, Your Honour knows that in some provinces the gasoline tax is fairly high. In some provinces the tax on automobile licenses is fairly high. In some provinces liquor is not sold very cheaply.

National Highways-Mr. Pouliot
It is a good thing to sell liquor, because it is a great source of revenue for the provinces, and that money can be used for the public benefit especially by building roads. That is the policy which was followed in Quebec by Mr. Perron when he was minister of roads. He very boldly imposed his policy upon the government to which he belonged, and I believe it was a success. Some years ago, for instance, the farmers complained of the bad state of the roads. Indeed the roads were bad, and in some parts of the country it was very hard to motor even in the month of May. The roads were very muddy and full of holes. But now they have been improved on the basis of fifty per cent lent by the government to the municipalities, and after the roads were improved they were taken over by the provincial government. That is the new policy to which I have just referred. In some parts of Quebec the roads are taken care of by the provincial government, as the burden has proven too great for the municipalities, and Mr. Perron, who was then minister of roads, should be congratulated on this policy. I do not know whether the same policy is followed in the other provinces; I speak only of what I know and I believe this is a very wise policy.
I would not be surprised, if we vote in favour of the resolution at present under discussion, that the provinces complain that the federal government is infringing on provincial rights. The leaders of some provinces are very touchy on that point.
Tasche-reau.

My hon. friend is just
repeating the word that was uttered when last year I asked my hon. friends who was the greatest man in the Conservative party. The same name was repeated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when he paid a very nice compliment to the Premier of Quebec by saying that he was the greatest Liberal-Conservative in Canada. At that time he overlooked the fact that the hon. member for Richmond-West Cape Breton was sitting behind him.
It is rather dangerous to deal with such a delicate matter as this. I believe there is in the constitution nothing that empowers the federal parliament to approve such a resolution. Moreover, if parliament votes in favour of such a resolution, many provinces may complain that the federal government is infringing on provincial rights.
fMr. Pouliot.]

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fervid eloquence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and his somewhat bombastic criticisms of some of the members, it requires no little courage to rise at this time in support of the resolution, but I should like for a moment just to scan the arguments put forward by the minister in opposition to the resolution itself.
In the first place-and I am taking them perhaps in order of priority of importance -naturally the argument is raised that it is contrary to the terms and provisions of the British North America Act. I have been looking over those provisions with some care since the commencement of the debate, and I can find in the British North America Act nothing which specifically places highways under the sole jurisdiction of the provinces. It states that projects of a municipal character are solely under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but it does not exactly classify those subjects nor does it definitely state what might be contained within the limits of those subjects. On the other hand, in discussing the powers of the federal parliament it states that lines of steam or other ships, railways and other works of a character affecting the interests of the community as between one province and another or between one province and other provinces, shall come under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. I would be inclined to say that the weight of evidence may be fairly well divided, and that we could consider a highway of the class we are now discussing as one of those works which approach in character steamship lines and railway lines and would become works of such a nature as to bring about communication between one province and another, rather than limit them solely to objects of municipal concern.
I was, however, struck by one statement of the minister which I felt was hardly accurate;
I mean it was hardly an accurate interpretation of the act itself. The Minister of Finance informed us that the field of taxation as between the federal and provincial authorities was strictly delimited, each having its own responsibility within its own field. I might call his attention to this fact, that while it is true that the field of taxation which may be explored by the provincial authorities is strictly delimited, no such limitation is placed upon the field of taxation at the disposal of the federal parliament. The federal parliament is given full scope. Every means of taxation which the imagination of man may devise is at the disposal of the federal parliament and for such purposes as it chooses to use

National Highways-Mr. Speakman
the money. So I would say that the minister hardly gave a complete or accurate definition as to the taxing powers of the two bodies.
I come to another point, to a very fair question indeed as raised by the Minister of Finance. He said, and with some justice, that speakers from various parts of this side of the house had given the impression at least that their interpretation of this resolution varied in many particulars, and he instanced three distinct propositions which we appeared to have in mind in discussing this resolution. One was the filling up of comparatively insignificant gaps between the existing highways. Another suggestion was that some of us had in mind the building of an entirely new trans-Canada highway, probably a hardsurfaced road that would be available in all weathers. The third suggestion was that some of us were asking the federal parliament to make grants to the provinces for the purpose, among others, of constructing marketing roads, and the minister invited us to interpret the resolution.
It is, of course, impossible for me to give the interpretation of this resolution as it exists in the minds of various members of the house. I can, however, give the very definite interpretation which I myself attach to the resolution. I have in mind something like this: that the federal parliament should make certain money grants to the provinces, under which the provinces would construct highways under terms and specifications as outlined by this house

I refer to the provisions of the Highways Act of 1919. In order to come within the terms of that act, the highways had to be constructed according to specifications outlined by the federal road engineer. I had in mind that the same provisions might be embodied here: that the highways constructed by the aid of the federal grant should come up to certain engineering specifications and should be so devised and so located as to form ultimately a part of a national highway system. I believe that if the grants were made with these .provisions attached, we should find ourselves in a few years in possession of that towards which we are all aiming-a complete trans-Canada highway entirely within the boundaries of our country, each provincial unit forming a definite link with the next provincial unit, so that the whole would make a complete national highway system.
The further suggestion was made that some of us desired federal grants for the purpose of constructing marketing roads. That, to my mind, is not the purpose either of the resolution or of those members who support it. We
have this in mind, however, that if assistance was given by way of a federal grant towards the construction of main highways, it would leave the provinces in a position where they could themselves properly take care of the marketing roads. Indirectly in that way, perhaps. the marketing roads might be assisted, but it would only be indirectly, and it would leave the entire responsibility of providing marketing roads to the provinces and to the municipalities, where, to my mind, this responsibility belongs.
I simply wished to bring before the house these two or three considerations. First, that constitutionally, as I interpret the British North America Act., there is no definite prohibition of the federal government's building a highway. On the contrary, highways as we know them to-day, in the light of modern conditions, would more nearly approach that class of subjects which are definitely committed to the jurisdiction of the federal rather than the provincial authority, because as we view highways to-day they do form, in essence, a means of communication as between one province and another, and as between the several provinces.
The second thought which I had in mind-
I am repeating this merely for emphasis and clarity-was that owing to the fact that the federal government has the definite authority to explore and utilize any and every means of taxation so long as any such means is not definitely prohibited, some responsibility should rest upon the federal parliament to expend for the general good of this country the money so raised.
I have listened to the arguments pro and con, and having in mind my own interpretation of this resolution, and the importance of the subject to the people of Canada-yes, having in mind the valuable nature of the work done under the provisions of the Highways Act of 1919-1 am heartily in support of an extension of that assistance to be carried out somewhat in the direction I have indicated.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
The resolution now before the house involves a principle that is not new. Prio: to coming into power in 1911, Mr. Borden, now Sir Robert, promised the people of this country that if the Conservative party attained power he would provide a measure of support for provincial highways. Elected in 1911, at the first session afterwards, in 1912, he introduced his measure. The then Minister of Railways and Canals, Mr. Cochrane, introduced the bill into the House of Commons. When the bill was read the second time, the
458	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Bennett
then leader of the opposition, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, raised a point of order as to the constitutionality of the proposed measure. The point of order was overruled by the Speaker, and the leader of the opposition then made a speech with reference to the bill itself. The bill embodied principles which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) tonight says were admirable, but which the Liberal party of that day thought objectionable. The measure as introduced provided that more money relatively might be paid to one province than to another because its necessities .might, be greater. That provision did not meet with the approval of the Liberal party of that day, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved an amendment which will be found in Hansard of February 23, 1912, on page 3643, and reads as follows:
That the bill be not now read, but that it be resolved that while the house is favourable to the granting of federal assistance towards the construction of permanent roads it is of the opinion that such aid should be given to the governments of the provinces for such purposes, and should be granted on a fixed basis similar to that now prescribed by the British North America Act and amendments thereto for subsidies to the provinces.
In the course of his remarks, Sir Wilfrid Laurier used these words which will be found in Hansard on page 3642:
We on this side of the house have no exception to take to this new departure for the purpose of aiding in the construction of highways out of the federal treasury.
New times, new men.
T'lis hiis not been the practice hitherto, but in the affluent condition of the treasury to-day, it may not perhaps be unwise that we should apply money in that direction. Moreover, the demand for highways is to-day more acute than it ever was before, and if it is intended to build new highways of a certain standard and to assist the various provinces in that respect, for my part I see no objection. The only exception I have to take to this bill is that any such exception should be made upon some rule provider! for in the bill, and should not oe left to the whim or caprice or favour of he government of the day. If this bill passes n its present form, any appropriations for ;his purpose can be devoted to one or two or three provinces, according as the ministry of the day may determine. In a matter of this kind there should be a principle of equity and equality applied as between provinces. What is to be the line that is to determine how the money shall be expended?
Then after discussing that he says:
Now, what shall that principle be? For my part. I submit that the only principle for the expenditure of such money is the principle to be found in the British North America Act, which in section 118 provides that the moneys paid out of the treasury to the various provinces shall be according to population. This 
provision was amended subsequently, complaint having been made that the allowances to the provinces were based simply upon the census of 1861. There were several conferences of the provinces, first in Quebec and then in Ottawa, commencing in 1887, all protesting that the allowances made to the provinces were not made on the principle of population, but on the population as it was in 1861.
He closed by saying that the basis of population was the sound basis on which grants should be made. You will therefore observe that Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1912 was wholly in accord with the principle enunciated by Sir Robert Borden and his government that aid should be given by the Dominion to the provinces for the construction of highways, and he moved his amendment by asserting that the house as a whole was favourable to that view. Before I leave that, may I say that the measure passed the House of Commons; it was amended in the Senate; the House of Commons did not agree with the amendment and repassed its measure, except for some trifling verbal amendments; and the result was the measure was not enacted.
It was contended that the distribution of the moneys should be made according to the population of the provinces, and in the Senate that was affirmed by a majority, it being contended that to permit the ministry of the day, or the governor in council, which is the ministry under another name, to make appropriations out of a sum granted for highways, would be to place a powerful weaipon in the hands of the government which could be used for purely political purposes. The Senate reaffirmed that principle on two occasions, with the result that the legislation then introduced in the House of Commons and passed by the government of Sir Robert Borden did not become effective.
However, in 1919, when a Union government was in power, a measure was agreed to, and a resolution was introduced in the House of Commons. It will be found in the journals for 1919 at page 76, when notioe of motion was given by Doctor Reid, then Minister of Railways and Canals, and at page 92 the resolution came up for consideration and wa3 finally considered later. It will be seen there that notioe of it was first given on the 19th day of March, 1919. I need hardly remind the house that it was not until June that the present Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Crerar) resigned from the then administration. So that on the 19th day of March, 1919, the present Minister of Railways, being a member of that administration, was responsible for the introduction into the House of Commons of a resolution, which resolution provided for federal aid being given to pro-

National Highways-Mr. Bennett
vincial highways. It also provided that the distribution of that money should be in accordance with the population of the several provinces. To that extent it yielded entirely to the contentions made by the Liberal party in 1912, that is, affirmed the necessity of federal aid being given to provincial highways, and adopted, population as the basis for distribution, for reasons which were obvious. The measure then introduced provided for a grant of $20,000,000 to be expended in five years for the construction of highways in the provinces under terms and conditions that were to be settled between the federal and provincial administrations.
That grant of $20,000,000 was expended in the provinces on the basis of population, except that a fixed grant of $SO,000 per annum was paid to each of the provinces. In other words the sum of $400,000 became available in five years to every province in the confederation, small and large, for the purpose of improving the highways in the provinces, and the balance of the $20,000,000 was in the five year period divided amongst the provinces on the basis of population. That was wholly in accordance with the views expressed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1912, which I have just quoted, and which views are embodied in the terms of his amendment to which I have directed attention. In 1919, the resolution having been adopted, the measure was passed by the House of Commons and the Senate and became a part of the law of the country. It. will be found as chapter 54 of the statutes for that year, assented to on July 7, 1919.
It provides for the distribution, as I have said, of $80,000 to each province per annum and the allotment of the remainder to the governments of the provinces in proportion to the population of the provinces as shown by the last census. The conditions under which the payments were to be made, were settled by agreement between the governments, and regulations were prepared and reports made to parliament as to the expenditure of the moneys.
The five years have elapsed. The whole of the money has been expended, and there being no further necessity for grants to be made to provide employment for the soldiers who had returned from the war-although the figure given by the Minister of Railways as to the number to be demobilized in 1919 was larger than the fact-the question now is: shall we continue the grants made in 1919? That is, not continue them in the sense that there has been no break in the period of the grants being available for the provinces; but shall we continue the principle of making grants from the federal treasury to the provinces to enable them to construct, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, permanent roadways?
I am wholly in accord, Mr. Speaker, with the terms of the resolution, and I believe the principles which governed in 1912 and 1919 are principles that are as applicable to-day as they were then. The conditions under which highways are being constructed bring that construction, not without but wholly within the British North America Act, so far as the Dominion is concerned. My friend the minister has challenged not so much the competency of this parliament to grant moneys in any way that we may desire-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all.

He forgets perhaps what his leader said last session, that it was " a thoroughly vicious principle " to appropriate public moneys to the provinces that they might expend as indicated by parliament. He has now not challenged the constitutionality of it, but he has challenged it as an act which is unconstitutional so far as the demand for it is concerned, and which he says can only be made a matter of grace and favour. Yet what was said by my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg seems to me to have singular appropriateness. The province has complete control over local works and undertakings, but there is a class of works and undertakings over which the provincial legislature has no jurisdiction, and over which this parliament has sole and absolute control, namely, lines of steam and other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs and other works and undertakings connecting a province with any other province or provinces or extending beyond the limits of the province. In other words, each province, as a province, can deal only with its revenues for the purpose of constructing a highway to the boundary of that province, but if it was desired to assist-and I take it that all parties are agreed that it is desirable to assist-in the construction of an all-Canadian highway-that by way of illustration- within Canada from the east to the west, this parliament would not only have jurisdiction to make a grant for that purpose, but it would fall within the exception to the exclusive powers of the provinces, and come within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. And, therefore, if it is desired that money should be expended for the purpose of linking the provinces one with the other, for the purpose of forming a continuous highway from one part of Canada to another, and we desire to subsidize it or in any way to assist, the granting of that subsidy is within the competence of this parliament, and consideration is given to it, just as consideration
In that case there is no adverse balance of trade with the United States.

There are invisible balances the other way which my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) has perhaps overlooked, and the total net balance may or may not be $250,000,000. I am not prepared to say within a few dollars or within a few millions, because in respect to that it has been found very difficult by the department of statistics to speak with any degree of certainty regarding the invisible items. We have interest to pay on obligations in the United States, some of them of a private character, and we have large operations on

National Highways-Mr. Bennett
the stock exchanges of New York and Chicago with respect to which it is very difficult to get accurate figures. So that the visible or invisible balance is something that is not easy to speak of with any degree of absolute accuracy. But I would like this house to realize-and I know sometimes we do not do it; in my own case I found it difficult to appreciate the fact-that the sum total of these small items paid by tourists amounted to the vast sum that I have just mentioned, representing, as I say, at least a quarter of a billion dollars. It meant money available to redress a trade balance that was visible and to that extent it became exceedingly valuable; it was one of the main factors in maintaining the Canadian dollar, and prevented it from falling at least below ninety-eight cents. As I said, I think it was a little lower than that in one of the border cites.
Under these circumstances, having regard to the fact that we must think of the maintenance of that enormous traffic, how can the provinces do it if one province maintains a poor road, another province a little better road, and the richer province a very fine road? When I was driving through the province of Quebec, I remember one of my companions explaining to me the good roads. He said: "Mr. Bennett, that is what you will call a whiskey road." I did not realize for the moment just what he meant, but what he conveyed to me was that the profits derived from the sale of intoxicants had been utilized for the purpose of maintaining the very splendid highway over which we were then passing.

Does not that apply to
every other province except Prince Edward Island, where they have no motor cars?

I see that my hon. friend is behind the times both in his question and in the statement it contains. There are motor cars in Prince Edward Island, and I am going to use that as an illustration in a moment. In the second place, the motor traffic has not reached the same volume in other provinces as it has in the great province of Quebec where you have a city of over a million people.
What about Ontario?
Ontario, perhaps, is comparable. Last year more than three times as many motor cars entered Ontario as entered the province of Quebec.

Did they not use their
profits on liquor for the purpose of making good roads?

They are not specifically appropriated for that purpose, and in British Columbia the distribution of a portion of the liquor profits is made to the municipalities, as my hon. friend knows.
I was just going to illustrate my own experience in Prince Edward Island. That province is a garden; the soil contains no gravel and the construction of roads there becomes almost impossible without the importation of material with which to build them. I recall that on a wet day in a motor car it was very difficult to keep to the road even with the aid of chains, because the wheels could not get a grip on the soil.
It is hard for statesmen to keep their feet in Prince Edward Island, is it not?

No, but it is somewhat difficult for them to keep their seats in Prince Edward Island, as possibly some of the hon. members nearby will presently determine. I am casting no insinuation at ail upon the hon. gentleman who aits to the right of my hon. friend. That condition illustrates admirably the point I wish to make. I remember meeting in Summerside a gentleman from New York who was travelling with his family in bis motor car, and spoke to me of the beauties of Prince Edward Island, its beaches and magnificent natural bathing facilities. He also spoke of the difficulties of motoring. The cost of creating a road in that province is out of all relation to the cost of creating one in Nova Scotia. You can build a gravelsurfaced road in Nova Scotia, where there are nearby gravel pits, for a reasonable sum of money. My friends from Prince Edward Island will admit that to do so down there you have to bring material from New Brunswick or Nova Scotia at great cost, not only for transporting it across the dtraits but also for distributing it t.o the roads themselves. Where we have conditions such as those, and where we are inviting tourists not for the purpose of taking their money from them but with the idea of offering them something in the way of scenery and in the way of conditions they do not have at home, to say nothing of the refreshments that may be obtained under proper conditions-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not in the island.

No, not in the same way. Under those conditions is it not reasonable and fair that this resolution should be adopted?
Some of the members from the western provinces will have an appreciation of what it
462	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Bennett
costs to build highways in their districts. For instance, in some parts of the province of Saskatchewan there is soil eight, ten or twelve feet deep without a sign of stone or gravel of any kind; it is an alluvial deposit. To build a road there is a most expensive undertaking.
It is because of these conditions, I take it, that this resolution is upon the order paper, and I believe that the money of this country can be devoted to no more productive end. I use the term "productive" in the largest and best sense of the term, as filling a great national purpose, the redressing of an adverse trade balance and the maintenance to some degree of the value of Canadian currency. I know of no factor more potent for that purpose at this moment than the tourist traffic, having regard to the trade conditions between United States and Canada. It is vital to the maintenance of that traffic that we should have these roads maintained with some degree of uniformity in the various provinces, and in my judgment that can be attained only if we adopt the principle which the Liberal party espoused in 1912 under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but which party alt that time interposed certain objections. Those objections were fully met in the legislation of 1919 and are embodied in the statute to which I alluded in the former part of my observations.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I support the motion before the house, with the utmost confidence that a measure of this kind will be and must be resorted to if we are to continue to offer facilities that will attract to this country a great asset, which plays so large a part in maintaining our currency at near par and in redressing the adverse trade balance between Canada and the United States.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has just drawn our attention to the occasions upon which the Conservative party has brought forward, as one of its policies, the question of aid from the federal treasury to the provinces for highway purposes. My hon. friend mentioned that before 1911 Sir Robert Borden had stated that if he were returned to power he would ask that an appropriation be made from the federal treasury to the provinces for the purpose of aiding the construction of highways. A little later on in his address my hon. friend mentioned that in 1919 the Unionist government had made a similar proposal, or rather had introduced legislation for a similar purpose.

Perhaps I should remind my hon. friend, with respect to the year 1919, that at that time the Unionist government had ceased to exist as such and had become the Conservative party, out and out.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) was a member of it at that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not at that
time. What I wish to draw to my hon. friend's attention is the significant relationship in the matter of time of these proposals to a forthcoming general election, either actually in sight or anticipated. In the year 1911 Sir Robert Borden was in the thick of a general election, and it was at the time of that election that Sir Robert Borden made the statement that if he were returned to power he would ask for an appropriation from the federal treasury to be given to the provinces.
It was in 1910 he made the observation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, he was getting ready for the election, and through the election he continued to make that statement, just as my hon. friend, when his turn comes, will take advantage of a general election to make a similar pronouncement.
And with similar results.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is quite clear from my hon. friend's remark that what he has in mind is the relationship of his proposal to a general election. That is the point I wish to bring out.
Not my proposal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In 1910 Sir Robert Borden anticipated a general election, and made this proposal to the provinces in the expectation that it might help to gain for him some measure of support, at the expense of the federal treasury.
He promised us our natural resources, too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And made many other promises as well. My hon. friend said that after the election of 1911, when Sir Robert Borden was returned, he introduced a measure implementing his promises.
At the first session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, and I hope my hon. friend and the rest of the house realize it was the first session only, and not the second, the third or the fourth session. My hon. friend tells us that at the first session.

National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
he had the support of Sir Wilfrid Laurier as well. May I ask my hon. friend why, when Sir Robert Borden was assured of the support of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the commons, he let the matter drop after the first session?
Because the Senate was in the control of the Liberal party, the vote in the Senate being 29 to 9.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was at the first session. Sir Robert well might have done what the present government has done; he might have reformed the Senate. However, it is quite apparent that after the first session Sir Robert felt to all intents and purposes he had implemented the promise he had given at the general election, and the road was smooth for some years. Sir Robert forgot about the aid from the federal treasury for highway purposes, from that time on.

There was the war in
between.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The war did not come until 1914.
The Senate was not reformed until 1918.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In 1919 we
see a similar performance. The Conservative government at that time, expecting that its life could not endure for very long, brought in a measure along the line of aid to the provinces from the federal treasury, for highway purposes. This was introduced in reality for no other purpose than to gain support at a general election. My hon. friend says "with the same results." May I say to him that perhaps his efforts at the moment in this direction will be ended with the same results as followed the measure of 1919.
We are coming to a time when hon. gentlemen opposite seem to think that another general election is looming up on the horizon,-
We hope so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
- and they are becoming very anxious to have something more in the way of promises which they can make at the expense of the federal treasury. That is the significance of a number of the orations which we have heard this afternoon from the other side of the house.
These matters must all be considered in the light of conditions existing at the time. In 1911, when Sir Robert Borden came into office, the country was not under the heavy load of obligations which it has to bear to-day as a consequence of the great war which has since intervened. Since Sir Robert Borden
introduced his measure there has been added to the public debt of this country on war account alone something like $1,680,000,000, a debt entirely unforeseen at the time Sir Robert Borden sought to give aid to provinces from the federal treasury. In addition to that, obligations have been taken from the shoulders of the provinces with respect to their railway debts and assumed by the federal government. If we had not this great burden to bear, in the meeting of which we are not assisted at all by the provinces and which falls exclusively upon the federal treasury, we might afford to be generous in making grants from the federal treasury. But we have to be just before we are generous, and in being just our first obligation is to begin to pay off the vast sums of borrowed money which were used for the purpose of carrying on the war and at the same time seek to reduce the taxes of the people, so far as they are needed for federal expenditures. I think it is correct to say that for every dollar which will be spent this year for federal purposes, 43 cents of that amount, or 43 per cent, will be paid upon obligations which have arisen directly or indirectly out of the war, obligations which no previous government had to face; for every $100,000 paid out of the federal treasury, $43,000 will go towards the payment of such obligations; and for every $100,000,000 paid out of the federal treasury, $43,000,000 will go in that direction. Not one cent comes from any provincial treasury to assist the federal treasury in carrying that obligation. It has been pointed out this afternoon that not only have we assumed this vastly greater obligation as a consequence of the war, but there is every indication that that obligation will continue to increase rather than to lessen. The expenditure on account of pensions is certain to become larger year after year, and a bill has been introduced at this present session regarding war veterans' allowances, which will further increase the demands upon the federal treasury. The provinces are not going, to help us to meet those obligations. It would be as just and as reasonable for the federal parliament to make an appeal to the provinces to assist us in the payment of these war obligations, as it is for the provinces to-ask us to meet their obligations with respect to construction of highways, technical education, or any other matter. We do not do it. Why? Because we recognize that with respect to matters of administration certain duties have been very wisely assigned to the provinces while other duties have been assigned to the federal government, and in the long run probably less confusion will be met with, and more progress will be made by each
464	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
government carrying on the the work which comes primarily within its particular jurisdiction. That is a principal which I feel should guide us in matters of this kind.
There is another obligation which has been assumed since the measure of 1919 was enacted, an obligation to assist the provinces in the matter of old age pensions. That contribution will amount to something like $3,000,000 this year, and is an obligation which did not exist at the time the highways bill was passed in 1919.
That leads me, Mr. Speaker, to make a further reference to the legislation of 1919. I think I spoke upon this matter last year, and speaking from memory at the moment I believe I cited at the time what was said by the Hon. Doctor Reid, who was then Minister of Railways and Canals and introduced the measure in this house. Doctor Reid pointed out that many men were returning from overseas who would not be able to find immediate employment and it would take some little time to re-establish them properly in civil life. He thought that it was important that there should be some public work upon which these men could be honourably employed for a considerable time, and it was upon that ground that an appeal was made to the house to assist the provinces in the matter of highway construction. A similar step was taken with respect to loans for housing purposes, and there were other purposes as well.
The second clause of the resolution reads:
And whereas in that year the Dominion government recognized its responsibility in this matter by a substantial grant, which grant is now exhausted;
May I say to the hon. member who has moved the resolution (Mr. Kellner) that the responsibility which was recognized at that time was not the responsibility which he sets forth in the premise of his resolution; it was not a responsibility with respect to highways, it was a responsibility to the men who had returned from overseas, it was a responsibility in the matter of helping to re-establish in civil life those who had served their country so nobly abroad.
One paragraph only is directed to that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I should have quoted first the first clause of the resolution. It is as follows:
Whereas the need for establishment of highways is greater than in 1919;
I cannot agree with my hon. friend in that statement, for the simple reason that since the year 1919 there has been a very considerable

highway development, a very considerable expenditure made upon highways. We are provided to-day with highways to a much greater extent than in 1919. Something like $20,000,000 has been expended on highways since 1919 under the one measure to which reference has been made. The highways have been improved to that extent by federal aid, but that is only a part of the total expenditure which has been made by the different provinces. Our highways are in an infinitely better condition to-day than they were previously, and, as the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) pointed out this afternoon, there is to-day extending from coast to coast practically a great chain of highways which link this portion of the continent from sea to sea. There remain hiatuses here and there which, however, are being rapidly filled up. The most important, as has been pointed out this afternoon, is in a section of the province of Ontario. It has been said over and over again to-day during the debate that this .year Ontario has had the largest surplus in its history since confederation.
Good government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not saying what the cause is, but I am citing the fact. This parliament, before it begins to meet its own obligations, is being asked today to give money out of the federal treasury for provincial purposes to a province that 'boasts tihat it has the largest surplus it has had since confederation. That is the feature to which we take strong exception in the proposal in the form in which it is now being presented.
Does the Prime Minister see no difference between provinces that have had their natural resources since 1867 and the prairie provinces that have not received theirs yet?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I must thank
my hon. friend for bringing up that point, because it reminds me of something of which I wish to speak. When my hon. friend (Mr. Adshead) was speaking a little while ago he mentioned the fact that the western provinces had not had their natural resources, whereas the older provinces had; but he did not tell us that they were receiving subsidies in lieu of resources and that to-day they are receiving in lieu of their resources subsidies which other provinces which have their resources are not receiving. My hon. friend may not be aware of that fact but it is a fact. To a certain extent, all of the provinces are receiving subsidies from the federal treasury, but the provinces that have not their natural

National Highways

Mr. Mackenzie King
resources are receiving in addition subsidies in lieu thereof, so that they have right along been getting money from the federal treasury to assist them in matters of the very kind we are discussing.
According to population.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not
worrying about population at the moment, but I think that is the case. Let me come to the other point which my hon. friend has also stressed, namely, the importance of keeping the country united from coast to coast. A highway may help to unite a country; it would certainly be an outward and visible sign; but as far as the union of provinces by means of transportation facilities is concerned, we have already on this continent the two finest railway systems in the world, and if means of transportation help to unite the different provinces they are being united by that method more effectively in this country than are provinces or states in any other country in the world.
But something more important than means of transportation, it seems to me is required, if we are to keep the country united. The real bond of union is the removal of all grievances between provinces and the federal government. The real bond of union is a bond of harmony and good will as between the different provinces and the federal administration, and in this regard great progress has been made by the present administration. When we came into office we found an unsettled condition in this country, a condition of unrest in all parts of it, a condition of unrest in the maritimes, in western Canada, in British Columbia, and arising in each case more or less out of some relationship between the provinces and the Dominion which it had been found impossible to have properly adjusted under previous administrations. We set to work to see what we could do in the way of removing those conditions which were straining the relations between the provinces and the Dominion.
In the case of the maritime provinces we had the matter investigated by a commission and we have acted upon its report. In connection with that report we have given to the maritime provinces increased subsidies which they are receiving to-day, additional money out of the federal treasury to assist them in meeting just such obligations as the matter of their highways and roads. We have done that already.
When we come to the western provinces, we have dealt with the question of the return to them of their natural resources, and we have dealt with that problem on a very 2419-30
liberal basis. We have made with Manitoba and Alberta agreements which have been presented to parliament. We have concluded also an agreement, not yet signed, with Saskatchewan. As between the Dominion and that province there remain some legal questions still to be agreed upon which are to be referred to the courts for a decision, but apart from that there has been reached with Saskatchewan an agreement very similar in terms to that which has been reached with Alberta. Therefore as regards the three western provinces we have reason to expect that before the present session of parliament expires, their natural resources will be returned to them, or rather, will be returned as soon as implementing legislation can be passed by the Imperial parliament.
In this connection may I say that while we are returning to the provinces their resources, we are doing more than that: we are agreeing to continue to those provinces the subsidies which were given to them in lieu of lands. We are going further even than that: we are agreeing to continue to the provinces the increased amounts which under the existing act they will become entitled to as the population of each increases. These all constituted extra demands upon the federal treasury. The federal treasury is giving up some of the sources of revenue which it has to-day and handing them over to the provinces.
