It is at the same time increasing the subsidies which it is giving to the provinces to carry on work of their own concern.
In British Columbia we are returning lands which for some time past that province has asked the federal government to return; I refer to land in the railway belt and in the Peace River block. These we are giving back and we are also continuing to British Columbia a subsidy to which she would not be entitled excepting for what we hope will be the action of parliament before the present session is over. Therefore I may say the condition with respect to grants from the federal treasury to the provinces has changed materially since this matter was under discussion before. We have assumed new federal obligations and we have renounced, or rather transferred to the provinces, certain sources of revenue and resources which from now on will serve their interests and should enable them to take on additional burdens in a way in which they have not been able to assume them before.
May I say just this one further word in conclusion? We have no desire in any way to do other than assume our full share of obligation with respect to any of these matters which relate alike in part to the Dominion

466	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
and the provinces. As the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has said this afternoon, we have an obligation with respect to building highways in the national parks of this country. In the national parks of the west the obligation is a very heavy, a very onerous one. We have assumed it at considerable expenditure. We are improving the highway system there. That is a federal obligation, and we are prepared to meet it. We feel that the provinces within their own areas, with respect to their roads, should be equally prepared to assume their own obligations.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) referred to a phrase which I used last year in describing a certain system, a system of raising money by one government and having that money spent by some other government. I described that particular system as to my mind being a vicious system. I am glad my hon. friend to-night was careful not to go beyond his reference to the system as such, because I noticed that in some of his remarks on the public platform, and certainly in the remarks of many of his followers, my hon. friends have gone very much further in their representations than they are prepared to go in this house or can honestly go in any place or at any time.

May I correct the right
hon. gentleman? On every occasion that I have referred to it, I have read from Hansard what my right hon. friend said, together with the interruptions of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) and myself, and my right hon. friend's answers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but my
hon. friend has linked up with these questions the representations of parts of his own speech and has left or has sought to leave on the minds of the people an impression concerning my statement which is wholly erroneous. I do not, however, want to argue at the moment concerning what he has been saying; I simply wish to make clear what I said and I hope that will be sufficient to avoid further misrepresentation. The misrepresentation of which I complain is that these hon. gentlemen opposite have sought to have it appear that I have been opposed to technical education, to the construction of highways, to unemployment relief and to those other provincial matters which in the past have been assisted by means of public funds from the federal treasury. Nothing could be further from the truth. The one other project I was trying to think of, perhaps the most important, was old age pensions. They have alleged that I was opposed to
rMr. Mackenzie King.]
old age pensions because, under the present arrangement they are paid in part out of grants from the federal treasury to the different provinces. I am not opposed to old age pensions. I have been foremost as one of the advocates of old age pensions from the very beginning, and I am proud to say that it is the government I lead which brought in the first measure of old age pensions in this country.
I am not opposed to technical education. I was the one who, as Minister of Labour, first brought into this house a resolution for the appointment of a royal commission to study the whole question of technical education, which commission made a recommendation that there should be a grant from the federal treasury to the provinces for a limited number of years, pending the time that it was necessary for the provinces to construct the buildings that were essential for technical school purposes and to enable the staffs of teachers to become duly qualified to undertake the work of teaching in technical schools. That was a measure brought in by a Liberal administration, and a measure of which I for one feel distinctly proud.
Similarly with regard to highways. I feel as strongly as any member of this house concerning the importance of highways and I would like to see a great transcontinental motor highway, but as long as we have to the fore certain obligations that can only be met by this government and will not be met by the provinces, we have to consider all such obligations first. As has been pointed out to-night, one of the most important of these obligations, one quite new, only recently to the fore, is the air mail service. I venture this prophecy here and now, that when we come to the appropriations for air mail service, hon. gentlemen opposite will be protesting that we are spending too much money for that service, and I will venture the further prophecy that when we get through these particular resolutions that demand additional grants from the federal treasury to the provinces, and begin to deal with the estimates which are now before the house, we will find exception being taken right along the line to expenditures which are all essential for federal purposes. When it comes to seeking to pass certain resolutions which involve extra payments from the public treasury to the provinces to meet their expenditure, hon. gentlemen opposite are united in their demands in that direction, but when it becomes necessary for us to seek the money to carry on the obligations of the federal government, hon. gentlemen opposite will be equally united in

National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
refusing to vote us the money that we need for that purpose. We have to face that situation. We know what we need for federal purposes, and we are determined to see that federal needs are supplied first. If, after federal needs are supplied, if after we have reduced some of the public debt and have reduced some of the taxation of the people of this country, we have money left that we do not know what to do with, with respect to any of our federal obligations, there will be time then to go into one or other of these numerous projects which hon. gentlemen opposite wish us to indulge in.

You can spend more
money in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, that is
quite true, but may I ask my hon. friend this: Does he regard Ottawa as the capital of this Dominion? Is he proud of his capital, or is he not? Does he expect to get from any province any contribution towards expenditures on the capital?

I am not so proud of it
that I would tear down all the buildings in town to build new ones.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will find lots of supporters to go that length with him.
May I draw attention, Mr. Speaker, to the perspective in which these particular resolutions must be viewed by the house. If this were the only resolution before us asking for a grant from the federal treasury to the provinces there might be some reason for us to debate the matter at great length, but this is only one of a dozen resolutions all of which are very similar in character. We had the other day from the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) a resolution which is before a committee of the house at the present time, suggesting that we should set up a system of intermediate credits for agriculture. We had a night or two ago from the hon member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphaii), a request that out of the federal treasury we should establish international scholarships and a chair of international relations in the different universities in the several provinces. To-night we have a resolution asking us to grant money from the federal treasury towards the construction of highways in the provinces. Next but one on the order paper to this resolution is a resolution of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich), which we shall probably have discussed for a day in the house, asking us to make additional grants to the provinces for technical education. Then there is a resolution of the
hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cot-nam) asking that immediate action should be taken with respect to the nationalization of the supply of radium. This would mean, I suppose, that the federal government would be expected to supply the provincial hospitals at its own cost. There is a little further on a resolution from the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) asking for a more equitable arrangement of the collection and distribution of the general revenues, implying that we should give up some of the present sources of our revenue to the provinces, notwithstanding that we are being requested to make th^se different additional grants to them. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) has a resolution that it is a national necessity that immediately certain railway outlets should be built from the Peace river, also involving further additional expenditure. My hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) has a resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of making grants to the provinces equal to one-third the cost of establishing, and to cover permanently such full time health units as may be organized.
And so it goes-aid to municipalities and provinces in the relief of unemployment, and all the rest. These are only the beginning. Once these demands are met, I suppose that as many resolutions for yet other purposes will come upon the order paper.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe any government or any country could possible carry on without some definite understanding as to the scope of its obligations in the matter of expenditure, and the limitations to be placed upon them. The scope-that it seems to me wise at the moment to consider is the one which, very wisely, was laid down in that much-abused British North America Act, which assigns to the provinces certain obligations, and to the federal parliament certain other obligations. We will do well, I believe, in the interest of provinces and federal government alike, each to have regard to our respective jurisdictions, and not to venture too frequently beyond them in making contributions from one treasury to another in a manner never contemplated by the constitution of our land.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to this debate, and I am verv glad indeed to notice that we have so many highwaymen in the house-I mean hon. gentlemen who are in favour of highways. I think that the house has a good deal of sympathy with some of the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Macken-

National Highways-Mr. Irvine
zie King). The government's task is a very difficult one indeed. They are on the treasury benches, and they are sitting there pretty tightly. They have to raise the money for all the expenditures of Canada. We appreciate that. We also are aware of the fact that we are in debt and that the government is charged with carrying on. We are prepared to remember all these things. The remarks of the Prime Minister, however, remind me of a parent who is unable to meet the demands of his children. One boy wants a pair of boots, another a pair of pants, another some toys. The father comes along and says, "We have to buy bread, and we have to pay the rent, so we cannot buy you boots and we cannot buy you pants. You will have to go without." We would say that that parent was not a good provider. The government says that it is in the position of having to take care of all the requirements of Canada as a whole, that it must look after the natural expansion of our industrial life, and at the same time pay off some of the country's debt, and therefore cannot assist in building highways. It should not be a very difficult thing for the country to find money for highways if all the prosperity talk that we have heard during the last two or three days be true. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that he dip into the prosperity can and take out enough to assist in building the highways as required by the resolution. I would suggest also to the Prime Minister that if we cannot pay our war debts and at the same time look after the natural expansion of Canada and attend to the interests of the people, then let the war debts go. I would rather let the war debts go unpaid than let the interests of the people go unattended to. If the Prime Minister will look at the number of people who pay income tax as compared with those who do not pay, he will get an idea of who is receiving the money that we have to provide for war debts. He will find that the many are paying the few. If we are going to devote the entire revenue of Canada to the payment of war debts, and neglect the building of roads and the other undertakings that he has mentioned, than I say it is in the interests of Canada to disregard war debts and look after the business of the people. I cannot charge the Prime Minister with creating those war debts, of course, but I believe they were unnecessary. Therefore I suggest to the Prime Minister that he use the credit of Canada in the coming years instead of permitting other people to use it, that he use directly by the power that he has, and not charge interest to the people of Canada for the use of their own 
credit; if he will do that he can easily get enough money to build this national highway in a very short time out of what he would save in interest.
The Prime Minister further said, after he had discussed the proposal of Sir Robert Borden-with which we are not particularly interested to-night, beyond pointing out that it was a very successful policy for the provinces; they all took advantage of it and liked it so well that they are asking for some more -after he had discussed that proposal he stated that it was a policy inaugurated by the Conservative administration. But in my opinion that is no reason why the Prime Minister should discount it at this time.
The Prime Minister also stated that this resolution comes from the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). It does not. It is a proposal made by an hon. gentleman in this corner of the house, and this is the second occasion on which it has been moved by him. The proposal has been endorsed by the organized farmers of the west and by many other organizations. It does not come from the leader of the opposition.
I think the Prime Minister is surely a little in error when he says that the Dominion government has the same right to expect the provinces to raise a part of the war debt as the provinces have to expect the Dominion to take some financial interest in the building of national highways. I do not believe that that statement is very fair to the provinces, and upon reflection I do not think the Prime Minister will repeat it. When he reflects that the Dominion government at the present time receives a very considerable revenue from the taxation of cars coming into this country I think he will realize that his government is standing in the way of the provincial governments obtaining revenue from car licences, gasoline taxes, and so forth; for he is aware that there are less than half as many cars in Canada as there are in the United States in proportion to population. I think it is fair to assume that if cars were as cheap in Canada as they are in the United States, as they would be if the tariff was abolished, our people would probably buy them in the same ratio as their neighbours to the south. If they did, the provincial governments would get a great deal more taxation from the augmented sale of gasoline due to the larger number of cars in operation, and consequently would be in a better position to carry on highway construction. So as a matter of fact this government is standing right in the way of the provincial governments carrying on this work.

National Highways-Mr. Kellner
Now, I think it has been demonstrated in the course of the debate that the need for highways was never greater than it is at the present time. I believe it has been shown also that to assist in highway building is an obligation of the Dominion government, an obligation that has already been assumed to some extent, and that being so the British North America Act goes by the board in this case and can no longer be allowed to stand in the way of the continuance of this aid. I think it was the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who pointed out that the Dominion government already was doing a great deal towards the construction of these highways, after of course he had argued for some time that it was not the business of the Dominion government to do this work at all. He pointed out that the Dominon government had been doing and was going to do a good deal more in this regard by taking charge of the roads in the Dominion parks, and so forth. Well, would not it be monev well spent for the Dominion government to go still further with this expenditure so as to receive the full benefit from what they have been expending on the Dominion parks and what they have already expended under the previous arrangement? I think that would be good business for the Dominion.
One thing which has not been emphasized very much was brought out by the mover of the resolution. The unemployment situation in Canada is bad; it is even worse than the Prime Minister will admit, and apparently, it is worse than the Minister of Labour is aware of. In fact those hon. gentlemen were content to point out that employment in Canada had reached its highest point this year. But they did not take into consideration the number of young people, born in Canada who went to the labour market last year and found no opening, nor did they give us the extent to which unemployment has been increased by the extraordinary number of our young people coming into the labour market. As a matter of fact our unemployment situation is very serious. Now, here is a proposal which undoubtedly would be of great assistance at this time. We are passing through a period of depression. It may be a very brief period -I hope so-but if the government ever intends to make any expenditure along the lines of this resolution or similar lines, now is the time to do it to alleviate the unemployment situation; then when prosperity is real rather than imaginary we could slow down a little on the expenditure. I hope that the Prime Minister will vote for the resolution even though he has spoken somewhat against it.
Is the house ready for the question?
Mr. Speaker-
I have to inform the house that when the mover of the resolution now speaks he will close the debate.

The wording of the resolution is apparently unfortunate, because, judging by what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and some of his colleagues have said, I think 'that had it been worded a little more to their liking they would probably have adopted it. However, as far as that goes, I think the resolution is worth adopting even as it appears on the order paper.
There is one point with regard to which there seems to 'be confusion in connection with the 1919 legislation. The Prime Minister said the Canada Highways Act was introduced primarily to assist the Conservative party in the elections that were expected to come, and did come, very shortly after. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar) said the measure was introduced to assist unemployment. I have looked the matter up and it appears that neither of 'those hon. gentlemen is quite right. When the resolution was introduced in 1919 Doctor Reid said:
The resolution is important for this reason; we all know that for many years the government have been expending large amounts of money on railways and waterways, and we feel it is now necessary to expend money on our highways in order to provide proper transportation facilities for the public. A good deal has already been done Towards improving our highways, but much more must be done.
Later on he said:
The principal reason for it is not so much to give employment as that the work is of the utmost importance. and should, we think, be proceeded with in order to facilitate transportation.
So that the argument of Doctor Reid at that time was not on unemployment at all, it was assistance to highways.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) told how the federal government is at the present time spending considerable sums of money in the building of roads through the national parks. I do not know why that should be mentioned, because I am at a loss to understand who would spend money on those roads if the federal government did not do so. It would be going very far to suggest that the federal government should have the privilege of going into a province, marking out a park, setting it aside, and then asking

National Highways-Mr. Kellner
the provincial government to build a road through it. But, as a matter of fact, I do not think they are building all the roads through those parks. I am under the impression that in Jasper park at least the Canadian National Railways have spent a considerable sum of money on that road; therefore I do not think the federal government has built it in its entirety.
The argument was advanced that no reason had been given why the federal government should provide money for the building of this highway. I think a very good case has been made out to indicate that if they did make an expenditure of money on this highway the government in a very few years would not be out anything. Apart altogether from the economic standpoint, let us consider the expenditure from a national point of view. Reference has been made to the money now being spent in Ottawa, and reasons have been given why this should be made a city of beauty for the people of Canada. But let me point out that the person from western Canada who desires to come to Ottawa to view these beautiful buildings must, if travelling by motor car, go through the United States to get here, and that is not at all desirable from a national standpoint.
AVhen we take the vote in a few minutes, I have no doubt that the resolution will be defeated just as it was last year. My recollection is that when the Prime Minister was in the west he told the .people out there that if they wanted assistance badly enough it would be given. I am going by a report that I saw in the newspaper. The Prime Minister shakes his head, so I shall have to withdraw that. However, I am sure I am right when I say that there are many people in this country who do not desire the government to move along any line so much as they desire them to move along the line of highway assistance.
